This reporter goes on to say that this is information gathered from a survey of farm conditions in that county. A report is published bearing date of April 5, 1943, with respect to dairy cattle, and showing that while there was an over-all increase in cattle production amounting to 7-1 per cent as of December, 1942, as compared with the same date in. 1941, most of the increase was in respect of young stock and beef cattle, and very little of it in respect of milch cows.
The report of the Ontario department of agriculture dated April 13, 1943, reports that there was a decrease of 4,400 milch cows in Ontario during the preceding year. Numerous individual press reports would seem to indicate
that the shortage of man-power on Ontario farms is producing or is likely to produce a shortage of foodstuffs such as Ontario raises.
Earl Kitchener, secretary of the Ontario Milk Producers' Association, speaking at Listowel on December 19, 1942, said that in several instances surveys had been made, all indicating that farmers were planning to cut down the production of dairy produce. In one district in which normally there were 10,000 milch cows, more than a thousand farmers had gone out of the production of milk entirely.
I understand that the Department of Agriculture has asked this year for an increase in the production of sugar beets. On May 22, 1943, the Ontario department of agriculture reports that there will be a marked reduction in the acreage of the sugar-beet crop. This is only one of the many conditions prevailing in Ontario, which indicate, or at least may be considered to be danger signals, so far as production is concerned.
The minister has assured us that there is likely to be a plentiful supply of potatoes. The report of the Ontario department of agriculture dated May 27, 1943, states that the yield from the early crop of potatoes will likely be at least twenty-five per cent below normal. With respect to the total crop it states there will be a considerable reduction in the aggregate acreage sowed to potatoes. I understand that the government is asking for an increase of 10-7 per cent. At this point I would say that regardless of the thousands of tons of potatoes being stored in one province, the citizens of Toronto-and I do not know the conditions in any other city-are faced with difficulty in securing a supply of table potatoes and, in numerous instances, are paying the price of seed potatoes in the purchase of potatoes for table use. That is the actual position in Toronto to-day.
If there is not a shortage, by reason of the number in storage, then somebody has fallen down in the matter of distribution. These potatoes are not available at ceiling prices to consumers in different Ontario centres.
On April 30, 1943, the London Free Press reported that after an extensive investigation in Huron, Bruce and Middlesex counties, and after talking with numerous farmers, they are of the opinion that field crops, including grain, will be at least twenty per cent below those of 1942, and that there will be an embarrassing shortage of feed grains and other dirt crops.
Just one further item, in support of my contention that there are danger signals on the horizon, so far as the production of agricultural products in Ontario is concerned, and that unless the man-power situation is faced immedi-
Man-Power-Mr. Noseworthy

ately there will be increasing dangers of shortages. A report issued by a dairy authority on May 11, 1943, shows that cheese production for January, February, March and April, 1943, amounted to 11,684,530 pounds, as compared with 27,629,310 pounds for the same four months in the preceding year, indicating a decrease of fifty-seven per cent in those four months. Apparently some emergency measures must be taken to meet this situation.
I suggest that no one on Ontario farms wants to see our armies stripped of personnel, or their efficiency [DOT] reduced. It has been suggested to me that there are two available labour pools from which farmers might draw. The minister's statement that only 4,000 applications had been received from farmers in Canada for farm help is, I am assured, in no way indicative of the present need for farm help. My opinion is that farmers have reached a conclusion somewhat as follows: What is the good of applying for farm help? Already 4,000 applications have been filed, and these are not being filled readily. "In any case", says the farmer, "if I get a man from the city or from the army, I cannot afford to pay him a proper wage, if he is any good, or a wage which will enable me to retain his services . In Ontario, farmers are becoming disheartened with the struggle. They are beginning to ask, "What is the use of trying to maintain the production level which we have tried to maintain during the past years?" The government has not told us how many divisions it is expected will be sent overseas or how many thousands of reserves will be required to supply these divisions when they get into action. We are told the number of men available in the home defence forces and that it is the policy of the government to raise another 25,000 during the year for home defence.
Most of the farmers with whom I have spoken feel that it would be in the interests of the war effort if something more helpful could be done by way of releasing some of these men now being trained for the defence forces. I am assured that the present regulations with regard to the release of men from the army, a copy of which I have under my hand, does not begin to meet the needs of the farmers of Ontario. There is, I believe, a pool of labour in industry. The speaker who preceded me referred to the hundreds of thousands of workers who have been drawn from the farm into industry, and into the army. I have not the figures of those who have gone from agriculture into industry, but they must run into the hundreds of thousands. 
With the process of levelling off that is going on, wTe hear continually of hundreds- in some instances it is as high as 1,500-of workers who are being changed from one industry to another or who are being laid off in one industry and then being placed in another by national selective service. I should like the minister to tell me how many men have been laid off at the John Inglis plant during recent months and how many have been reemployed. I was told by labour leaders on Sunday that there are still several hundred of the men who were laid off at this plant who have not yet been placed by national selective service.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend
suggesting that they should be sent to the farm?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am suggesting that in the interests of the war effort those men who have had farming experience might be placed on the farm. There are many thousands of young men in industry who have had agricultural experience. They were taken from the farm last winter and placed in industry for the winter months with the understanding that they would go back to the farm in the spring. The minister probably knows the actual number who have gone back, but my information is that there are still many thousands who have not yet been returned to the farms from which they came.
If help is to be given to the farmer, either from industry or the army, the government will have to face up to the necessity of subsidizing farm wages. Executives of farm organizations assure me that there is no other way of overcoming the shortage of farm help. If the farmer is paid a subsidy he will be able to compete with industry and the armed forces in the payment of his help. That is the first suggestion I would make. I am told that it would help immeasurably if the farmer were able to obtain the gasoline he uses for his tractor tax-free. I am speaking particularly of Ontario where the tractor is used on small farms. Many farmers feel that present prices do not permit them to buy gasoline for use in their tractors.
Another suggestion that has been passed on to me is that the government subsidize the purchase of feed grain as soon as seeding is completed. If this were made sufficiently attractive it would induce farmers to maintain or increase their herds. I am told that many farmers are reducing their herds. There

Man-Power-Mr. d'Anjou
will be a plentiful supply of grass this season, and many farmers are likely to reduce their herds to a point where they can feed them without having to buy feed grain. Relief of this kind would help, not only in the production of meat but in the production of eggs and other agricultural products. I pass these suggestions on to the minister, not as a schoolteacher farmer but on behalf of the genuine dirt farmers of Ontario.
Mr. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a
few words on the matter at present before us. This question is vital to both the province of Quebec and the whole of Canada. I represent a farming constituency. I have never failed, ever since I have held a seat in this house, to fight on every occasion for the gallant agricultural class. Therefore, I am grateful to the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) for having moved this resolution, which gives me another opportunity of taking the defence of the farming class whom I humbly represent. I am glad to pay this tribute of gratitude to the hon. member for Temiscouata. He has always been, in this house, the gallant protector of the agricultural class and the upholder of every worthy cause. Some hon. members blame him for his numerous and lengthy speeches. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscouata never fails to uphold the rights of his fellow-countrymen or fellow-citizens. I would wish this house had twenty-five members as energetic as the hon. member for Temiscouata, for then the present government would go through the mill time and again.
Frankly, it must be admitted that the agricultural class of this country is in a pitiable and discouraging situation. There is so much truth in this statement that, in my own riding, some farmers, unable to procure the help necessary for the operation of their farms, have had to sell or leave them. However, we hear on the radio, we read in the press passionate pleas begging the farmers to produce more and more, to increase their output. But they are being refused the help they need so much. The farmer is deprived of his sons who are sent to military camps, while the father, often far advanced in years and unwell, remains alone on his farm. Through discouragement, he very often forsakes his agricultural calling.
The agricultural class, as I so often repeat in this house, deserves every consideration on the part not only of hon. members, but also of the government and is entitled to all possible encouragement from them. A
short while ago, an hon. member from Ontario stated that victory could not be attained without soldiers. If soldiers are essential to a victorious conclusion of the war, these troops must be properly fed and our farmers and their sons must be placed in such a position that they can till their land. It has been said that the land is the great provider. If our soldiers are to be earnest and energetic defenders of their country they must be well fed.
The present government have unfortunately deceived the farmers of Canada. Last year, large headings in the newspapers proclaimed that the administration had decided to grant exemptions from compulsory military service to farmers and their sons. This campaign was launched just before the holding of the plebiscite to incite farmers and their sons to vote "Yes". Once the subterfuge had had the desired results, exemptions were completely refused to them. Personally, hundreds of cases have been brought to my attention and I have voluminous files on the subject. I have applied everywhere to secure postponements and leaves, not exemptions, mind you, for they were unobtainable, in spite of the deceptive promises. I have applied for postponements or leaves for farmers' sons whose presence was absolutely essential on the farms and never have I been successful in obtaining practical results.
Why do not the present government, who draw their inspiration from the Union government of 1917, set up in the county seats, exemption boards or appeal boards whose members would be the worthiest citizens of the locality and whose duties would be to decide whether the farmers' sons whose exemptions are requested are really more useful on the farm or in the military camps? In 1917, the town of Rimouski had an exemption committee comprising the mayor of the town and two well-known citizens of my county, honest and sane people, to whom the farmers, accompanied by their sons, addressed1 their requests. These requests were carefully examined, and when the members of this board decided that the farmers and their sons or helpers were more useful on the farm than in the army, they granted them an exemption. The present government, and I repeat what I have already said, is even more nefarious than the 1917 government which was condemned so severely by the Canadian electorate at the time of the 1921 elections.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
In that case, why don't
you go over to the other side of the house.
Man-Power-Mr. Jaques

Mr. d'ANJOU:	Following the example of
the hon. member for Temiscouata, I will tell the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Leelerc) that the constituents of Rimouski elected me to this seat in the house, and here I stay; I will also speak as I see fit even at the risk of displeasing the hon. member.
Mr. Speaker, I really believe that the motion introduced by the hon. member for Temiscouata came at the right time, and I hope that the government will seriously consider all the reasons which he gave as well as those which were suggested by the hon. members who spoke before me in support of his views. We want to win the war, and yet, we will not allow the farmers to produce what is needed to feed not only the civilian population, but our soldiers as well. When justice is sought for a farmer, the same answer is always given, and that is the crowning argument; we are at war! The end of the war will not mean the end of the world; Canada will still be in existence. But unfortunately, as the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lizotte) said a while ago, a Canadian author may write "La terre qui meurt." Farms will be deserted in the other provinces just as in the province of Quebec. My province is primarily agricultural, and it will be greatly affected. Therefore, I shall be pleased to vote in favour of the motion introduced by the hon. member for Temiscouata who has, in all circumstances, and I say it once again, defended the rights of his fellow-countrymen and of his fellow-citizens; I hope that the number of members who are conscious of their responsibilities and who fully understand the position of the agricultural class will be broad enough to support the motion.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a
point of order. A while ago, I made a remark to the hon. member when he said that the present government was more nefarious than the union government of 1917. Such is not my opinion, but if it be the opinion of the hon. member, why does he not take his seat on the other side of the house?
Mr. d'ANJOU:	In that case, I am not of
the same opinion and it does not concern the hon. member whether I stay on this side of the house or go over to the other. Mr. Speaker, I shall be delighted to support the motion of the hon. member for Temiscouata.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that if I were to suggest gold mines as a field for finding the needed farm labour I should be told that I did not know what I wTas talking about. It would seem that once a man works in a gold mine he is unfitted to work at anything else. At least that has been hinted in this house, and I might suggest that the same is true of those who think in terms of gold.
At a time when farmers by reason of war necessity have been deprived of a great deal of their labour, they have also suffered great losses in machinery, because they can neither buy new machines nor obtain repairs for their old machinery, and there is beyond question a considerable loss of efficiency on the farms in consequence. I might mention a case that was brought to my attention this session.
A number of elevators in my riding, at the request of their patrons, the neighbouring farmers, had intended to install machinery for cleaning grain and they went so far as actually to buy the grain cleaners, which are now and have been for the last eighteen months or so lying in the elevators. But they cannot get permission from the construction controller to install the cleaners because, as I am informed, and as the late controller of construction told me, they cannot spare either the labour or the materials from the war effort. That also is the answer which has been given to me in Alberta by the machine companies. They say that they cannot get the machinery or repairs for the farmers because the manufacturers cannot get the materials to put into the machines.
If that were strictly true, I would not be speaking to-night; but it is not true, because an immense amount of iron and steel, and other materials which the farmers could use, are at the present time and have been since the war started wasted in the mining of gold. I simply wish to say this just now. Surely in this time of war the needs of the farmers, that is, the needs of those who must produce the food of the nation, and the food of the allied nations, should come before the needs of gold miners.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
We certainly owe the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) congratulations upon having raised in the house a matter of such great importance. I cannot refrain from congratulating also the hon. member for

Maji-Power-Mr. Dorion
Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Dupuis), who did not hesitate to join the hon. member for Temis-eouata, even if it did not please his colleagues.
Many members of the government looked scandalized this afternoon when this question was brought before the house. It was as if a crime was being committed.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend is serious when he says that we were scandalized and that it was a crime. That is not fair.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I said that many of them were scandalized, though this debate might interrupt only for a few hours the consideration of the war budget. When any hon. member raises a question, even of primary importance, such as this one, the majority of the members sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker, successfully hide their discontent. The whole trouble in this matter, as in so many others, comes from the fact that since the beginning of the war the government has not been able to foresee the consequences of its acts.
As regards. the raising of men, the government has acted as if it were the same thing as the production of goods. They decide to raise 10,000 men and orders are given to those concerned to raise 10,000 men, without asking whether this can be done without endangering agriculture, the mines or any other essential industry. That is why we are faced to-day with a problem which is almost without solution.
I believe the government should be grateful to the hon. member for Temiscouata for having brought this problem to the attention of the house to-day. We must not forget that agriculture entered this war as one of the most depressed industries. Farmers *were unable, owing to the prices they received, to pay the wages which their labour was entitled to expect. By its very nature, agriculture is not an industry which can suddenly turn over to new methods and increase its output, as many of the mechanized industries can. However, we have seen the government spending millions upon millions of dollars to build war factories. But how many millions did we give to agriculture to improve its means of production?
I was amazed not long ago to learn that some industries are allowed twenty per cent and even fifty per cent depreciation during the war. Are these industries more essential to the war effort than agriculture? The only thing the farmer demands is to keep on the farm those who can help him to make the land produce as much as possible.
One thing is certain: the farmer will not make money through this war; and this cannot be said of many other industries. It is urgent that the government take the necessary means to improve the situation. And do not forget that with this state of affairs, with all the restrictions imposed upon the farmers, their morale is getting lower and lower, and this may be the worst of all. It may be a good war effort to spend as many millions as possible; but we must not forget that the basis of all our war effort is agriculture.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my speech will be a short one, as usual. I am not in the habit of taking up the time of the house where I consider that, speaking generally, a considerable amount of time is wasted. I do not hesitate to state that the session should be over by now. I simply wish to support the motion of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), because certain statements are deserving of utterance. Various views have been expounded to-day. I approve of some speeches and disapprove of others. If, for example, the farmers are behind in their seeding, it cannot be attributed to the scarcity of manpower. The rainy season is to be blamed. Contrary to what the last speaker has said, the farmers make more money in periods of -war. However, their income is still not large enough to allow them to compete on the labour market and pay two or three dollars a day for help. Butter would have to sell at from 75 cents to SI a pound to permit them to do so. The farmers are unable to pay such high wages.
I specially wish to draw the attention of the house to the trouble we are faced with regarding the men called up for training. The government have amended their man-power policy. Since March, 1942. this policy is more liberal than heretofore. Before that time it was deemed advisable to call up every farmer because it was considered that they might help to protect their own homes. Our views have altered since that time. To-day there is no trouble in getting postponements for bona fide farmers' sons, but difficulties are met with when we are dealing with those who have been called up in 1940 and 1941.
In my riding, I have come across many very deserving cases. I shall call two or three of them to your attention. Last winter, a seventy-year-old widow, who has only two sons, requested that I try to get leave for one of her sons who had been called up before 1941. After months of work, I finally was successful in securing leave for that young
Man-Power-Mr. Leclerc

man who, however, did not reach the farm, where only one son remained, until late in the spring. On this farm, there were 25 milch cows and anyone who knows something about agriculture, realizes the amount of work the care of these animals represents. I may state in passing that, in Shefford, we have the largest herds in the province of Quebec. The mother exhausted her strength in attempting to help her son. Finally, in June or July, I believe, the other son, who had been called up for training, was granted leave for a few months. He went back to the army in the fall. This year, after some delay, I was again successful in securing further leave for him. He is now on the farm, having obtained leave of absence for three months. Mr. Speaker, that is not enough. He should have been granted at least six months, for, in my opinion, a farm on which there are 25 cows, as well as sheep and other animals requires at least two good men. The truth of this is evidenced by the fact that, at the time when there was only one son on the farm, although the latter includes a woodlot, they had to buy fuel wood.
I may mention another nearly similar case, where 25 cows were kept. The father and mother are at least seventy years old. Both became ill, and a nurse had to take care of them. They had only one son at home. This spring, I obtained a postponement for him but as every one will admit, two men are scarcely enough on a farm of that size, and at least three would be required. Those two men can scarcely do all the work and they should remain on the farm the whole year round. In the cases I have just mentioned, the men are not French-Canadians, but English-speaking people.
I could mention many other cases. A dairy farmer told me on Monday morning: "I keep 30 milch cows, but I have only one son at home". Moreover, this farmer sells his milk in town. All those cases deserve our consideration and I ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to consider them most carefully. Farmers' sons whose services are essential on the farm, whether they were mobilized in 1940, in 1941 or even in 1942, are entitled to the same consideration shown to those who are liable to be called up this year and who are practically exempted.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am not going to occupy the time of the house as an effective means of hampering our war effort. My purpose is not in any way to detract from that great cause. But I do wish to say a few words upon this subject before it

is allowed to pass. I believe the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) did! well to bring this matter forward, because it is very timely.
A while ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) asked1 the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) where the shortage of food would be. I do not think it takes any stretch of the imagination to know where a food shortage may occur.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
It just depends upon
what kind of imagination one has.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is the trouble with the Minister of Labour; he has not a good imagination.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Coming from my hon. friend that is a compliment.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
That shows that I can at least pass the minister a compliment when he has it coming to him. There is no question as to where the shortage of food will be; it will be right here in Canada. One does not have to use imagination in that respect. The shortage is here now; otherwise there would be no necessity of rationing, and rationing is being extended all the time. I am not objecting to that, because it is the proper thing to do if there is a scarcity, but it is great folly for us to ration food without making any concerted effort at the same time to increase production.
So far as the shortage of food is concerned, the minister has in mind, as we all have, that Canada is raising more foodstuffs now than she ever did before. Nobody is denying that. But we have committed ourselves to definite obligations to countries overseas, obligations which we cannot escape. Therefore we must raise enough in addition to take care of our own wants, and I maintain we can do that without any difficulty if we have a proper man-power policy.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has asked for greater production this year of all foodstuffs; and, speaking in the house some little time ago, he expressed the opinion that there was nothing in the way of reaching that objective, so far as man-power is concerned. I hope he is right, but I greatly fear he will find1 himself mistaken before next fall comes round1. Just because we have on hand a good supply of certain commodities, such as wheat, I do not think we should sit down contentedly and say that all is well. This year, I believe we are in for a setback, even in regard to wheat; and if we should have a disastrous season, with the commitments we

Man-Power-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
already have for overseas delivery, we in Canada are going to find ourselves rather short even of wheat, as well as other commodities.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
So long as we do not
run short of talk we shall be all right.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
If we do,
I am sure the minister will make up any shortage; he has done very well in that direction so far; but that is about all he has done, for the onus of this whole question falls upon the shoulders of the Minister of Labour. I am n>ot going to blame him personally; as I said once before, speaking of the strike in Montreal, he was asked to do an impossible thing, and I explained why I -made that statement. I do not intend to go further into that matter now.
Some of the difficulties we shall face this year will come as a result of the late seeding which, together with the shortage of manpower to put in the crops, will make the harvest exceedingly late. Then, again, there will be a man-power problem; the harvest will be so late that there will be a great rush, and there simply will not be enough men to take it off. That is a problem we might as well face now, ini order that we may make some preparation to meet it. I believe this whole question could be handled most efficiently if we would all face it honestly. Let me explain what I mean by that, and I do not think I could do better than quote the words of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) as reported at page 3275 of Hansard for yesterday:
. . . I am not running an air force to go farming, but to fight overseas and to train here. If a man enlists in the aircrew he enlists of his own free will and he must go through the training for a most important job of work, costing us $25,000 if he is a pilot, $27,000 or $28,000 if he is an observer or navigator and so on. I do not think we can afford to let him go away on farm leave. I do not know whether the committee will agree with me. but so long as I have anything to do with the air force, either it will be an air force or they will be farmers and will go back to their farms. I do not wish to have a double-barrelled organization, running farms and an air force at the same time.
I wish to congratulate the minister on his frankness, and to say further that he has been staunch in his stand in that regard ever since the beginning of the war. That is the proper stand to take. You cannot fool around with this question; and I think if the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) would come out with a similar statement we would begin to clarify this matter.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What about the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am just coming to that. There is no use ini talking; neither in the air force, the army nor the navy can you have a man here to-day and gone tomorrow, andi the people in these departments are not to blame. That blame properly should be placed upon the mam-power policy of this government; that comes under the Minister of Labour, and that was what I meant a moment ago when I said that the responsibility definitely fell upon the shoulders of the Minister of Labour. There is no manpower policy so far as agriculture is concerned. The Minister of Agriculture has also been placed in an impossible situation, and now he is trying to get out of it as best he can. I remember that I was talking to the chairman of one of the selective service boards in regard to agricultural postponements and he saidi, "I don't want to take these boys off the farms any more than you do, but here is the position in which I am placed. I get an order from Ottawa saying they want
25,000	men. Out here in the west, where am I going to get them? We have taken practically all the men we can get from the cities, though we can still pick up a few here and there. Anyone with an ounce of brains knows the only place we can get 25,000 men is from the farms, and as long as they tell me to get 25,000 men I am going to take them from the farms or any place else. If they don't like that, they can change the policy." That is talking straight, and there was no argument against it. There, again the responsibility was thrown directly where it belongs, right on the shoulders of the Minister of Labour, and whether or not he likes it he will have to accept that responsibility. When a man is taken off a farm and put into the army, apparently that is where he should be, and that is where he should stay. But if he is essential to agriculture he never should have been taken off the farm. Surely that is what the selective service boards are for.
If we look at agriculture in the proper light we must agree that agriculture is just as important as any other war industry in Canada. We have discovered the folly of saying, "Well, when harvest time comes we will send some of the school boys or school girls or what have you to the farms." We tried that experiment last year; no doubt the Minister of Labour did so in all good faith, in order to meet an emergency. These fellows from eastern Canada were sent to the west
3306	COMMONS
Man-Power-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
but, as the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) says, they could not take it. You cannot take a fellow from the city, I do not care whether he is a school boy or a full grown man, and put him on a farm at harvest time and expect him to keep up with the other men. It just cannot be done. I spoke to some of these fellows who were on their way back east last fall, and they acknowledged that they could not keep up with the work. It was not their fault; they just could not carry their end. It would be the same whether you paid them $7 or $8 a day. So that the farmers are reaping the benefit of our muddled labour policy, to the extent that ini my own constituency as much as ten bushels to the acre have been lost on account of mice. Who should be blamed for that? The farmers were not to blame; it was definitely the fault of the government.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The weather.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Not altogether.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The harvest was late last year.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Well, if the labour had been available the threshing would have been done, though a small portion might have been left over. I know of machine after machine in my own area that was running with only three, four and five teams when it should have had twelve or fourteen. The threshing was not completed in those areas, and the farmers were penalized to the extent of ten bushels to the acre. Not only that, but in a great many cases the grain was swathed, and not in the stook. The grain in the swath this year was spoiled, and some of it sprouted before it could be threshed, with the result that the harvest carried from last fall to this spring resulted in late seeding.
Coming back to the question of man-power, and as to whether it is efficient or not, may I refer to postponements from the army. Mind you, I wish to make it definitely clear that I am not disagreeing with the army or the air force. I think it is the height of foolishness for either the army, the navy or the air force to take in men and then be forced to allow them out for other work. But let it not be misunderstood that I do not think the boys who are essential to agriculture, should ever have been taken off the farms and put into the army, and those who are there now should definitely be put back on the farms, with instructions to stay there. I think the agricultural leaves from the army, the navy and the air force are handled in an entirely wrong

manner. In the last couple of months I have been convinced, from what I have seen, that once you begin to get a postponement for a young fellow in the army, the air force or the navy, and happen to write a commanding officer, or the boy writes his commanding officer, right then they begin to step on him. Delay after delay occurs, as was pointed out a while ago by one of the other speakens.
The boy who happens to be at the army or air force camp is first instructed to get affidavits. He has to write home to his father or mother and they have to run around the country getting these affidavits. Then they send those off to the boy, and he has to take the matter up with his commanding officer. And so the process goes on for three or four weeks. Then the commanding officer does not think he can let the boy go on the grounds stated. Then probably the boy, his father or his mother writes to their member of parliament, and the member takes it up through the department. By that time the boy is transferred, and probably he is sent overseas.
I have one case before me, one which came to my notice to-day, where that very thing happened. I started correspondence in connection with this matter last spring, when seeding first started. When finally I got a favourable reply from the department the boy was drafted for overseas, although he had not finished his basic training so very long ago. I have another case, right here, which occurred in connection with the navy, *where the same is true. In this instance the boy was drafted to another ship, and away he went. The father and the mother wrote saying they imagined there was no use in going on with the matter. This boy was told that, so far as the armed services were concerned, no more leaves were being granted, and that all leaves were postponed.
This is definitely interfering with agricultural production. I fear lest this fall, when it is too late, we shall find out that we are falling far short of our expected production. Then we shall have a catastrophe on another front. That is too serious to be overlooked. Now is the time to take action, although even now is quite late.
I have in my hand a letter from a different part of Canada, namely, from Quebec, and I find that in that province conditions are no different from what they are in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I should like to read a portion of this letter, in which

Man-Power-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
a lady writes to me respecting her son. She had been at a meeting at which the deputy minister of agriculture was present, and following the meeting she wrote:
I protested to the meeting that there was even then, October, 1941, a serious lack of labour on eastern Canadian farms and that we had been forced only a month ago to sell at auction the highest producing pure bred Holstein herd in Quebec. . . . We had a succession of men who either enlisted or were drafted.
And then at a later point in the letter:
The fact that dairy herds were being sacrificed was recalled. Doctor Barton answered this by stating that individuals might be forced to liquidate here and there but such animals were purchased by other farmers and continued to produce.
And then in brackets she writes "Mr. Gardiner's theory". The letter continues:
To-day my husband and I are alone on a 300-acre farm within 55 miles of Montreal. Our son, 18, is in the R.C.A.F. He is better off out of it, we think. The farm, I mean. Here he too would be alone. . . . We have about 15 head of stock and milk one cow for ourselves, feeding a couple of calves.
There was a great dairy herd destroyed. She goes on in the letter to point out that in that neighbourhood other dairy herds had to be sacrificed because the boys were taken away.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Did the boy
not enlist?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member asked that question, because I had just picked up the speech of the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), with regard to which I wished to refer to that very point. The hon. member asked if the boy did not enlist. May I refer for a moment to the statement by the minister:
If a man enlists in the aircrew he enlists of his own free will. . . .
That statement is absolutely wrong and misleading. This system of enlistment we have is the most scandalous that was ever put across a country. It is not enlistment in any sense of the word; it is coercion.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Order. The hon. member will recall the motion before the house is one to adjourn the house because of a shortage of agricultural man-power. The question of enlistments is certainly not within the purview of that question of man-power.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I was going to show the house that the method of taking men from the farms was the effect of that. The question was asked definitely and I intended to spend a second or so in answering it.
It is definitely linked up with the shortage of man-power on the farms, and I think I can prove that to Your Honour in a few minutes.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Before my hon. friend does any proving, surely when he refers to members of aircrew he must know they are the most courageous men who were ever born.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the matter.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Oh, that is all right; but you said they were coerced into aircrews.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I did.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend is not serious about that. He makes a charge against young fellows like that who are flying over France and Germany to-night.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Do not try to bring a red herring across the path like that. The minister knows better than to do that.
Why did most of these fellows enlist?- because we did not have the gumption in this house to say what we thought. That is the fact, and every member sitting here knows it. And a good many members sitting in the cabinet know it, too. If we had had-I was going to say the intestinal fortitude, but I do not think that is parliamentary-if we had had the gumption to go out and state a definite policy we would not have the trouble we are having to-day. These fellows who were on the farms knew they would be called up. It is happening every day, and it is happening even now. They know they will be called up, drafted out of the farms and taken away from essential industry. They know they will ibe drafted into the army, and so they enlist.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: My hon. friend knows we are not drafting people from the farms into the army at this time. My hon. friend knows that.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
They certainly are being drafted at this time. That only shows the confusion that exists, even today. With all due respect to the Minister of Labour, I do not think he is serious, because I am sure he knows the difficulty he himself is finding with this man-power policy. But in my judgment he will never be able to settle the agricultural problem until he straightens out that question.
These young fellows on the farm, who are most anxious and willing to stay there, who know they are essential to agriculture, who know their parents cannot get along without them, must make a choice, they must either enlist or be conscripted. Hon. members
3308	COMMONS
Man-Power-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
know the stigma that is attached to the word "conscription". If everyone physically fit had been conscripted and put where he was most fitted, put to his task under a decent and proper selective sendee, we would not have the difficulty we have to-day. That is what is the matter. We have not as yet a definite man-power policy.
I hope the Minister of Labour will be able to get some suggestions out of what I have to say. Here is another suggestion that will help to solve the agricultural problem if heed is taken of it. At this very minute we are entering into an unemployment period. That is what is happening right in the heart of war. Men in industry are being thrown out of work. At the Calgary Ogden shops fifty men were laid off at one time, and two hundred at another. Those shops are producing essential war materials, and yet a return tabled in the house shows that only fifty-three, if my memory serves me aright, of these men have been replaced by selective service. Something like sixty are on unemployment insurance, and selective service does not know where the rest are.
Some of those men were experienced agriculturists. Why did the selective service boards not get after them? The one lady to whom I referred to-night has one son in the navy; he enlisted because he knew he would be conscripted. The other boy enlisted in the army for the same reason. I received this letter only yesterday, and she tells me that they have six hundred acres which are not seeded. Does the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) or the Minister of Labour contend that we can reach our objectives in agricultural production with conditions like that? That is only one case and there are many more over the country.
I am not going to speak at any great length on this matter. If the Minister of Labour will be as frank as the Minister of National Defence for Air was, he will come out and say he knows where the difficulty is. There is no question about that; otherwise I do not think he would be occupying his present position. He knows he has been in an impossible position trying to operate under a two-way system. He will have to establish a man-power policy which will put these men where they belong and keep them where they are best suited. If they are essential to agriculture, put them there and see that they stay there. If they are in the army, you will have to take them out and put them on the farm.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is
not careful I will put him in agriculture.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: If the minister puts me in the Department of Labour I know I shall not do any worse than he has done.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: My hon. friend misunderstands me; I said I would put him to work on the farm.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem of the shortage of farm labour is not one that has risen over night. This problem is the direct outcome of the policy of the government for three and a half years and its failure to tackle courageously and intelligently the problem of the allocation of manpower. We are paying the price to-day in a threatened shortage of fuel and food. Four different ministers have had this problem tossed into their laps. The first one was the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who for a while was Minister of National War Services. It was then passed over to Mr. Thorson, who was Minister of National War Services for a short time. Then it was the baby of the present Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche), and finally it was tossed into the lap or on to the doorstep of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). He cannot be blamed entirely for the present situation because he has inherited it. But the problem is there, and it is always more difficult to solve a problem after three and a half years of muddling than it is if it is tackled properly in the first place.
We recognized at the outbreak of the war the need of and advocated an intelligently planned programme for handling this problem. On September 9, 1939, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) set forth in this house the views of this group. Discussing this problem, he said among other things, as reported at page 57 of Hansard:
We have tremendous resources. In modern war huge masses of men are being replaced by mechanized units which require vast quantities of supplies to maintain them in the line. Frenzied demands for the enlistment of more and more men, if granted, may defeat the very object in view, success in this struggle. This was to a more limited extent true in the last war. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for example, noted that condition in a letter which he wrote on May 15, 1907, to Sir Allen Aylesworth, in connection with the problem of conscription, in *which he said:
"There is a shortage of labour in agriculture and industry, in fact in every field [DOT]where brawn and muscles are needed, and in the face of this condition people there are still yelling for more men being taken away from occupations in which they are so much needed."

Man-Power-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
We have recognized that throughout the progress of the war there have been two extreme schools of thought with reference to the problem of man-power. There have been those who have cried for an ever-increasing army who could talk of nothing else than conscripting men and putting them into the armed forces as though that in itself would solve the whole problem. We have maintained that to do that would be to overlook the fact that we have certain commitments for the production of war materials and foodstuffs and that our effort must be a balanced effort rather than a one-sided one.
On the other hand there have been those at the other extreme who have sought to have almost total exemption for fanners and farmers' sons and who have wanted to use every possible excuse to deprive the armed services of man-power. We have dissociated ourselves from that point of view. We have never believed that any special class or group should have special privileges. In our opinion that is class legislation, and class legislation of any sort is nefarious and harmful. The point of view we took was that we wanted an intelligent plan for the allocation of man-power. First of all we should find out what is our total available man-power; how many physically fit men there are within certain age groups. Our man-power pool is not a bottomless pool; it has definite limitations. Our first task was to find out what that was, and we asked for that repeatedly. Registration was supposed to provide that information. It did not do so very effectively. Then, out of that pool of man-power we must decide first of all the minimum number of men that would be absolutely necessary to maintain our home economy-to run our railroads, our mines, our factories and our foundries.
*Next we must decide what was the absolute minimum necessary to grow the foodstuffs which we ourselves required and sufficient in addition to meet the commitments which we have made to Britain and our allies. After we have decided the numbers that were needed at home and how they should be apportioned among these needs, we must decide what available man-power we had for the fighting services and how they should be allocated as between the army, navy and the air force. But that has never been done. Since the outbreak of the war, what there has been is a competition between the different departments of the government for the services of the same man. It did not matter what the man was doing, whether he was on the farm, in industry or in a mine. The army was asking for him; so were the air force, and the navy; munitions factories were beckoning to him; the coal mines wanted him in the mines; the railroads
wanted him on the railways. All the different departments of the government were competing with each other for the services of the same man, and at the same time the Minister of Agriculture was setting a programme for the farms of this country. In other words, the policy this government was following was the policy of laissez-faire. The policy which this government followed in peace time it follows now in war time-the policy of doing nothing until public opinion makes you do it, and then do just as little as you have to do, and do it too late.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And do it the wrong way.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What happened under that policy? The law of economics naturally took men from the low-paid industries into the higher paid industries. Men drifted from the farms into the munition factories, from the mines into the shipbuilding yards. All the time men were moving from the low paid industries into the higher paid industries. Also a large number of men went into the armed services. The result of it all was that on the prairies particularly, many of our rural areas were already completely denuded of man-power long before the government brought in compulsory military service. As a result of this unplanned confusion we find that Canada after three and a half years of war finds it has more men in non-essential industries than it had a year and a half ago.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The last available figures in January showed that it was true. The minister can give his figures.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I shall be glad to give them when discussing man-power.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The second thing that happened was this. After three and a half years of war we find the government asking the agricultural population, with
395,000	fewer men on the farm, to produce more foodstuffs than we ever produced before.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Are we not asking all our people to make a similar effort? And they are doing a pretty good job at that.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
They are. But I am trying to find out whether we have not gone beyond the limit in what we are asking our farmers to produce when we have 395,000 fewer men on the farm. We are asking them to produce quantities of foodstuffs that we would have thought a few years ago it was impossible for them to produce, even with hundreds of thousands more men on the farm than we now have. The result of it all is that to-day in Canada, one of the greatest
3310	COMMONS
Man-Power-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
agricultural countries in the world, we are rationing meat; we are rationing butter; we have some restrictions on cream, and in certain cities of Canada potatoes are unobtainable. If we had told that to anybody in the House of Commons three and a half years ago they would have said that such conditions were impossible.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Is it not because we are trying to feed the British people?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: No; that is only part of the story. We are not exporting beef or butter to Great Britain.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Cheese.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
What we are shipping to Britain is only part of the story. There is something more, Mr. Speaker.
At the beginning of this session I made a plea to the Minister of Agriculture in which I said that unless something was done in connection with the man-power situation on the farms we would face actual food shortages in this dominion in the next twelve months and might not be able to meet our food commitments to Great Britain-and it is very important that we do. The Minister of Agriculture answered in a very eloquent speech, but there was more eloquence than logic in it. He said that last year we produced more than we had ever produced before and with less manpower. That is true, but it was because, first of all, we had the best climatic conditions right across Canada that we had had1 for the previous twenty years. Such conditions may not be duplicated. Second, it was done at the expense of the people on the farms whom we asked to make superhuman efforts. Old men, women and1 children-I saw them last fall out in the fields shovelling wheat and pitching stooks.	[DOT]

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Pitching stooks?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Some farmer!

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is not hard to conceive if you know what the figures mean. It can be understood by anybody who knows about the shifts in our industrial economy, part-time workers in the cities and so forth.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
It is not
only our industrial economy, may I point out to the minister?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And in agriculture.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
In Votes and Proceedings of March 22, 1943, I find that in Saskatchewan, which is not an industrial province, the number of persons registered for employment was 2,769. That was at a time when it was difficult to get workers on the farms and difficult to get men to work in the coal mines in the southern part of our province.
Let me review what the government has done to meet the shortage of agricultural manpower. The first thing the government did was to pass an order in council, P.C. 2252, on March 23, 1942, which was supposed to freeze men on the farms. The fact is, of course, that this did not keep men from being called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act, although it was intended to do so. The best proof of that is found in the figures which the Minister of National Defence put on Hansard the other day, as reported at page 3031. I quote:
The intake of new personnel into the army for the fiscal year 1942-43 by military districts, based on telegraphic reports from the districts, is as follows.

Man-Power-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
Then follow the figures. The total is 74,204, who were taken in during the fiscal year from April 1, 1942, to March 31, 1943. That year pretty well comes within the period since the order in council was passed. What do we find? In spite of the fact that it was an order in council which purported to prevent men from being taken off the farms, we find that in military district No. 12, which is Saskatchewan, nearly 7,000 men were taken off the farms and put in the army. And when we compare that with other military districts we find that Saskatchewan is the third highest in Canada, the only other districts which are higher being No. 2, with 10,908, and No. 4, with 15,886. That is an amazing thing.
If one needs further proof one has only to look at the table which I placed on Hansard at page 2920. That table showed that although in Saskatchewan 22,119 were called up, only 8,041 were granted postponements. When the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Lalonde) this afternoon said that he had been handling 1,200 cases for postponement from military service and that more than half of them had been granted postponement, and when I look at administrative division F, Quebec, and observe that out of 26,565 on call, 21,474 were granted postponements, I begin to understand something of the 1,200 cases referred to by the hon. member for Labelle.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I will give the hon. member much more interesting figures than those when we have the man-power debate.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I shall be glad to get them, but to me these figures are startling. In Saskatchewan 22,119 men are called and 8,041 are granted postponement, and in Quebec 26,565 are called and 21,474 are granted postponement. And Saskatchewan is a province which is almost entirely agricultural, a province wherein order in council P.C. 2252 was supposed to have been enforced in order to prevent men from being taken off the farms.
The fact is that it was not applied, and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) is correct when he says that the men who were administering these boards were put in a dilemma, being told by the military authorities, on the one hand, that they wanted so many men, and by the government, on the other hand, "You are not to call farmers off the farm." Well, they had to take them off the farms, or they could not meet their quotas. If one needs proof that the order in council did not work, one has only to look at the interpretative letter sent out last January,
which shows that the government itself became alarmed at the extent to which farms were being denuded of the essential manpower if they were to produce the quotas of foodstuffs which the country had set.
When that did not meet the situation the government tried another measure. It was announced with some fanfare that men in the army were to be granted leave, and most people got the impression, through public statements which were made, and announcements over the radio, that this really amounted to something. But I fear the public were badly deceived. It did not affect more than an infinitesimal number of men. Look at the regulations and see who are eligible to receive agricultural leave. I think it is worth while putting it on the record:
Agricultural leave may be granted to personnel of the Canadian army serving in the following formations and units:
1.	Personnel on the strength of home war establishments district depots.
2.	Other personnel on the strength of the district depots, less those awaiting dispatch to basic training centres and those awaiting allocation after completing advanced or trades training.
3.	Personnel of Veterans Guard of Canada who have completed individual training and who can be spared from the duties on which their units or detachments are employed.
4.	Personnel of units employed on operational duties less those earmarked for overseas service. Such personnel must have completed individual training before being granted leave, and the number granted leave must not exceed five per cent of the unit strength at any one time.
Let us review these exceptions. First of all. a man cannot be granted leave if he is taking basic training. In other words, the ones most recently taken off the farm and whose parents are finding it most difficult to get along in their absence, are the very ones who cannot come back for spring leave.
Those awaiting dispatch to training centres and those awaiting allocation after completing their advanced or trades training cannot be granted leave, and even where they may be granted leave, the number granted leave must not exceed 5 per cent of the strength of the unit. And before a man can be granted leave he must have the approval of his commanding officer, which in turn must be endorsed by the district officer commanding and the general officer commanding. Well, of course, under these regulations the provision that the men in the army would be granted leave to do farm work has had little or no beneficial effect upon the scarcity of farm labour.
Before I sit down I wish to suggest that there are three things that ought to be done. First and foremost, the men now on the

3312	COMMONS
Man-Power-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
farms, men who are engaged in agriculture, should be kept there. The minister said a moment ago, interrupting the hon. member for Bow River, that men are not being called now. I cannot speak for the other groups in the house; but there is not a member in our group from Saskatchewan who does not get letters every (week-one might almost say every day, but I think I am safe in saying every week-with regard to men who are still being called off the farms in Saskatchewan, and who have made application for postponement and in some cases had their applications rejected. That is the first thing. These men ought to be kept there, not because they are farmers. I do not want any man to be allowed to shirk his responsibility because of his occupation; but if the country decides that, in order to feed this nation and our allies, a certain amount of foodstuffs must be grown, then it is our job to say to these people, "Your task is to produce these foodstuffs, and in doing so you are doing your part toward winning the war, just as much as though we had put you in uniform or put you in some other field of service".
The second thing which the government ought to do is to consider very seriously how they will dispose of the 68,228 men who are known as home defence personnel or "R" recruits called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. A great number of these men are off farms. I do not think it is being too optimistic to say that the danger of invasion of this country has receded to some extent in the last twelve months, and that if the invasion of Europe takes place the danger to this country will recede proportionately. It seems to me that the government must make up its mind what it is going to do with these men. Sixty-eight thousand men is quite a sizable pool of manpower; and, unless the government decides that it is going to convert these men into General Personnel and send them overseas, a great many of them ought to be returned to the farms, at least temporarily, if not permanently.
I agree with what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said, that you cannot have an army that is farming one day and fighting the next. So far as the general service personnel is concerned, I think that is correct. But here is a body of nearly seventy thousand men. The Minister of National Defence said that 25,000 more are to be called in the next year. That will be over 90,000 men who cannot be sent out of Canada. A great many are farmers or farmers' sons, and I think the government will

have to make up its mind either to use them as soldiers or to put them back on the farms.
As I said to the minister the other night, it was my experience last fall to see in the province of Saskatchewan young men taking their basic training, most of them off the farms, husky, brawny specimens out doing route marches, within a stone's throw of women and school children out working in the fields. It seems to me that the situation is ridiculous and that, if this country is to be faced with a food shortage, and if because of the lateness of the spring we need manpower, there is a pool of man-power that could be utilized.
Just one other suggestion I make to the minister. A large number of people have gone out of agriculture not into the army, but, as he knows, into industry, and some of them into non-essential industry. I know many of them who have gone to take more lucrative jobs; you cannot blame them for that, but they are jobs which do not contribute to Canada's war effort. I think a country which has assumed the responsibility of saying to some men, "You must go out and risk your lives for this country", ought also to take the responsibility of saying to other men, "We do not think you need to be waiting on tables or serving in stores; we think, since you came from the farms, that is where you ought to go." That will mean, of course, making certain adjustments. We cannot ask a man to leave a job at $125 a month and go to work on a farm at $60 a month. In some cases it might not be a sacrifice for him, if he is a single man, but if he is a man with a wife and family, it would be a very serious sacrifice indeed; and one of the things the government should take into consideration would be the advisability of treating these men who would be taken out of non-essential industry and returned to agriculture in the same way that we treat the man in the army, namely, pay his dependents an allowance, in addition to whatever he himself earns on the farm.
The argument will be, of course, that we would be paying different groups of men different pay. But we are doing that every day in the army, the air force and the navy. Two men may be marching together in the same platoon; one man single, the other man married, with several dependents. The total amount of money they are receiving out of the public treasury is different even though the service they are rendering is the same. It is one of the anomalies which comes out of our war; and when the government ask a man to do a certain thing which they

Man-Power-Mr. Picard
think he ought to do, they must accept the responsibility for looking after his dependents. I suggest that if the 220,000 men who have left agriculture and are said to be in industry are to be returned to the farm, the government should give serious consideration to setting up a dependents' allowance for those men who have families, so that, should they return to work on the farms they will know their families will not suffer by virtue of the fact that the government has asked them to make their contributions in agriculture rather than in some other part of our war effort.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Speaking on February 17, as reported in Hansaard at page 499, I concluded my address with the following words:
Let us not forget that the land is the first element that enters into the question of production. Farming is the primary industry and the most essential in carrying on a war, because the best trained men, -with the best and most modern equipment, cannot fight on an empty stomach.
I hold the same view to-day; but, because of the importance of this question I have decided again to take a few minutes of the time of this house to express my views on the problem.
On that same day I had asked the government to examine-
.	.	. the difficult situation in which some
farmers find themselves at this juncture. They do not know how to plan their production for the next year. They do not know where they will stand as far as help is concerned. On the one hand they are advised by the Department of Agriculture to produce more and more, which is good advice; on the other hand they face mobilization orders and varying interpretations in each district by the mobilization board. They do not know where they will be, if they are without the help of their sons or their farm hands. So far as production is concerned, they face a shortage in certain supplies which they need.
Prior to that, a year ago, on February 12, 1&42, if I may be permitted again to quote myself, I stated in this house, as reported in Hansard, at page 529: I
I admit readily that it would be hard to uphold that the agricultural class should benefit by special treatment that is not granted to other classes of people who do their share of war work.
I meant by that the same thing as the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), that, as a class, if their production were not needed, if we were not at the moment in a war when the need for more food was present daily, it would not be just and fair to state that one class in all the population should benefit more than another. But it is not just because they
are farmers, but because at this moment the farming industry is the most important, after our armed services and our war munitions factories that they should get special consideration. As I stated before, the army cannot fight on an empty stomach; I said at the same time:
The primary consideration is the service rendered to the country by the land tiller and the necessity to maintain or raise the production of food in order to help feed Britain, and, above all, to maintain Canada's health and vigour by proper diets, ensured by increased supplies of food. Therefore what appears to be important is to maintain a sufficient number of experienced men to cultivate the farm lands of the country. Although I am a layman in agriculture, I imagine it could be very easy for experts in that domain to determine how many men are needed to farm land of a definite number of acres with a given type of equipment and a certain number of head of cattle and hogs, and so on.
At that time somebody told me that this was not a practicable thing to do. I now know that there are experts of the Department of Labour who are doing this very thing. They are analysing the food situation, the situation on the farms, the productivity of certain lands, the number of people needed on different lands. I have met some of these experts, and I think they are doing a great job. They were very much surprised when I told them I had been criticized for having said that it could be established how many men would be needed on a given farm in different parts of the country. If you have flat lands which can be cultivated easily with modem implements, in the west, that would be one thing; in Ontario and Quebec it may take a greater number of men for the same number of acres. These experts are, I know, at work at the present time, and we shall soon see that they can produce results.
In the course of the same speech I stated further:
It would be quite easy then to state that a farm of thirty acres operated with horse-drawn implements with fifteen head of cattle, three horses and the usual small poultry yard, needs so many men. The owner, with three boys of military age, whose farm would fall under a category considered to need three men, and who is still able-bodied, would be allowed to keep two sons on the farm and -would give the third to the armed services.
Or to agriculture, to serve as a farm hand in another section of the country or in his
own district.
This classification of farms could be fairly accurately established, and the decisions of boards of the war services department could then be arrived at with a maximum of security against favouritism and law-evasion.
I think the importance of agriculture during this war is better established than probably
Man-Power-Mr. Picard

at any other time in the history of our country. I should like to read a sentence from an address by Hon. Herbert Hoover to the conference of mid-west governors on March 15 of this year:
Germany in 1914 produced about eighty-five per cent of her food supplies despite the blockade. Her war leaders were sure they could ration the population down fifteen per cent, and therefore had no anxiety about food. They neglected the food front. In three years, Germany was dangerously short of food. In four years, mobs were demanding bread and the emperor's head. And Germany weakened on the military front.
The lesson, we should take from this statement by Mr. Hoover is that during this war, while perhaps in many branches of agriculture we are one of the largest producers, we should not relax our efforts but should increase our production and1 do as much as we can, not only to feed ourselves but also to feed our allies and to anticipate the demands that will arise when the invasion of the continent takes place. Commenting on this statement by Mr. Hoover, the New York Daily Mirror of March 16 had this to say:
That lesson is that food production and distribution must be put on the same footing as the production of munitions.
I think that is one of the elementary truths we should realize at the present time. Then this newspaper went on to offer certain suggestions, which fortunately we have already adopted in our country. They said an immediate survey of their food resources was indicated. In a moment I will show that this already has been done by our Department of Agriculture. Then they stated that the responsibility for food production must be concentrated in one authority, because in the United States many people in addition to the secretary for agriculture have something to do with the production, control and distribution of food. Here we have control boards and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). In my opinion the Minister of Agriculture should be made supreme in the control of the production and distribution of food in this country. Not only because he is capable of doing that work but because if this were done we would have the advantage of putting all branches of agriculture under one head, to be directed under one jplan.
As I stated a moment ago, those were two suggestions in regard to the United States, offered by a newspaper in that country. Here in Canada we have made a survey of our food situation and a new programme has been drawn up. I have in my hand a booklet

entitled "Objectives for Canadian Agriculture in 1943", containing a foreword by the Minister of Agriculture, from which I quote:
It is a challenging programme. It calls for larger quantities of foods than Canada has ever undertaken to produce before-particularly meats, dairy products, eggs, fresh fruits and vegetables. These foods are urgently required to meet Canada's needs for the civilian population, for the armed forces in Canada, for ships' stores, for the Red Cross, and for export commitments to Great Britain and others of the united nations.
Each year since the war began, farmers throughout Canada have contributed notably to the war effort by increasing their output of those food and fibre products called for.
Then the minister paid tribute to those who voluntarily entered that field, and went on to say that all those who joined the ranks of the farmers deserved the same credit.
Let us look for a moment at this programme and at the reasons why we should now consider agriculture in a different way from that in which we have considered it previously, and I quote not from the words of the minister but from the pamphlet drafted by his department concerning these objectives for agriculture in 1943:
When war came in September, 1939, there was an abundance of almost every kind of farm product. In the case of certain staple products there were large surpluses. Disposition of these at profitable prices had been a problem for some years. It was not surprising, therefore, that there should be little concern about food supplies.
Just in passing I may say that this might explain why a couple of years ago there was less interest shown by members of other parties or from other sections of the country, and fewer requests made that agricultural man-power be spared and left on the farms. To-day it is consoling to have people from all parts of Canada join with those of us who a few years ago stood almost alone in asking that special consideration be given agricultural needs in regard to mobilization. Then the report goes on:
With the invasion of France, Belgium, Holland, Denmark and Norway in the spring of 1940 the situation changed very considerably. Supplies hitherto available, particularly from Denmark, were cut off, but accumulated stocks of certain foods were large and these had to be worked off before additional supplies were required from overseas.
