Subsequently arrangements were made to ship larger quantities of certain products, notably bacon and cheese.
Canada was requested to increase her shipments in these different staple products. With these changes that took place agriculture and industry in Canada had to face a

Man-Power-Mr. Picard
new problem, a new situation, and everyone in Canada had to accept as his first consideration the necessity of producing more in the way of food. We even had to make sure there would be sufficient raw material for the manufacture of farm implements, which at one time we were tempted to lay aside, and we also faced the need of maintaining more men on our farms. The report goes on to say:
Full employment and a very marked increase in payrolls, together with the increased consumption resulting from having more men engaged in the armed services, caused a very marked increase to occur in domestic demand. The combination of these various factors had by the summer of 1942, reversed the position as far as farm products were concerned. Shortages instead of surpluses began to threaten in the case of a number of products and the necessity of restricting consumption became evident in some instances.
Later on the report says:
It was not until the changes in our food requirements and supply position occurring in
1942	directed attention to the whole agricultural position that the need for increased production in a much wider range of products became apparent.
The rapid change that occurred in the food situation in 1942 made it necessary to take stock of our position and to make plans for
1943	that would ensure maximum output.
Then looking more particularly at the part of the country which I know best, as I have noticed most hon. members are tempted to do at times, I find that in the acreage seeded to oats, for instance, Quebec last year stood fourth in the whole country, having more even than Manitoba and one other of the prairie provinces. When it comes to hay, Quebec had the largest production, and was even asked to increase it by another 7 per cent. In 1941, 3,871,000 acres of hay were under cultivation, whereas in 1943 the goal is
4,29S,000.
AVe have the same situation in my province in several other fields. For instance, we see that this year in connection with hog production Quebec is asked for a 26 per cent increase over last year's production. \\Then it comes to dairy production we find that the estimated milk requirement for 1943 is placed at 8,500.000,000 pounds, which represents an increase of approximately 1,000,000,000 pounds over 1942. In this respect Quebec is the second greatest producer, and is asked this year to raise her production by 10 per cent.
AVe are the third province in the production of eggs and poultry', and again we are asked to raise our production by about 22 per cent, and we are asked to increase by 46 per cent the production of poultry' meat.
Then, going into the subject of potatoes, we find that Quebec is the largest producer. Despite the fact that it already has 172,700 acres under cultivation, it is asked to increase that area by ten per cent. This goes to show that the programme for this year in respect of all these different products will demand the work of more men than are usually required, with implements which are not more modern but have been used for two more years, and which cannot be replaced, and can be repaired only with great difficulty.
I should not like to speak at too great length respecting the hard life of the farmer- although some have done so. I know it is a hard life, not from personal experience, but because I have visited the people I represent. I know that in a climate such as we have in our part of Canada a great amount of energy is demanded, if our people are to carry on, and to face increased production when they are not sure of maintaining the same number of men they used to have for that type of production.
I should not like to change the rosy picture painted the other day by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood), one which I thought was very touching, and which I admired. In his statement he expressed a great truth about the farmer when he said that everything, of course, in connection with agriculture depends upon
. . . our philosophy of life, and the importance people attach to certain things.
He said:
The best things of life are the things which money cannot buy.
Then he went on to say:
Many farmers keep up their homes and gardens and obtain from their farms an income which goes a long way to sustain them satisfactorily, and they get many pleasures there which it is impossible to get in the city. If one appreciates these finer and better things of life, an efficient farmer on good land has an advantage over the average city man.
But despite this rosy picture, the lot of the farmer, under the difficult conditions he faces in certain parts of the country, is not an easy' one. For instance, we cannot compare acreages in western and eastern Canada, as some hon. members attempt to do, because the size of a farm does not necessarily indicate the number of men required to operate it.
I can assure the house my experience with the mobilization board has been that far from being too easy, as some hon. members have sought to insinuate, they have been just and
Man-Power-Mr. Picard

fair, and have taken into consideration all aspects of each case they have had under review, when men have been before them.
I have here, concerning the production of man-power, the text of-not a speech-a statement which was given over the radio.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Was the hon. member referring to me, when he said that insinuations had been made as to its being too easy?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I made no such insinuation. I merely pointed out that there was a great discrepancy between the number called in two different areas.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Better put him in a
museum.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the debate to-day. Much has been said, and said with emphasis, and much of it has been of value. I can assure you that I am not going to exhaust my forty minutes, because the subject has been well covered. I wish to point out one or two simple things as I see them.
The present agricultural emergency resolves itself, as I see it, into two things. One is that agricultural leaves have been granted, but instructions evidently have been given that commanding officers have no authority to extend those leaves. That is my understanding of it. The other important point is that seeding is already late, and many of the agricultural leaves that were granted have been used up and the men have had to go back into the service before they were able to do very much on the farms because of the bad weather. That seems to be the problem at the moment. All that has been said to-day is of much value with respect to the manpower problem generally and as it applies particularly to agriculture in the coming year. The season is late, and every day's delay or every two days' delay may mean the difference between a crop of ten or fifteen bushels to the acre, and a crop of twenty-five or thirty bushels. That is how close we are running now.
Just about a week ago I was travelling around a little bit in the constituency of Wellington North, not far out of Toronto. The hon. member for that constituency is not here to-day. Perhaps he is out there, helping the farmers to put in their seed. But I doubt it, because when I was there the whole country looked like the delta of the Nile. No seeding had been done at all and the farmers were getting tremendously worried. That seems to be the immediate problem.
I would just add this. The minister is going to reply perhaps very soon now. Personally I do not wish to hear any apologies from him. I do not want him to rise and take a lot of time in the defence of his department or in defence of the government.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The last speaker did that.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Yes; the last speaker did that. What I want, and what I think the house wants and what the country wants is a straightforward announcement of what the government is going to do now in order to ensure that crops will be put in without delay and be harvested in the fall. I notice
that the minister has his spectacles on. His desk is loaded with papers. His parliamentary assistant is sitting right behind him with another raft of notes on his desk. I am not concerned about the spectacles or the notes.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not detain the house very long.
An. hon. MEMBER: Hear, hear.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I think my hon. friend who says "hear, hear," will agree that the manpower question, while due regard must be had to the part which agriculture is playing in this war, is something that affects the industrial structure, the fishing industry, and the armed forces as well as the farming community. I did hope that this debate might have been deferred until I had been given an opportunity-

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Until after seeding.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I will come to seeding in a minute. I was going to say I had hoped that this debate would have been deferred until the whole man-power policy of the government could be reviewed iby the House of Commons, because in my opinion that is the sound and logical way of facing up to the man-power problem as it exists in Canada to-day.
I wish to be frank with some of my hon. friends. Under the War Measures Act we cannot change the weather, unfortunately, but I do pay tribute to the farmers of the country, and I would remind the house that while we have been talking to-day the farmers have been planting the seeds. An hon. member asks, what are we going to do now? I will tell him what the farmers in his own province have done. Eighty-three per cent of the wheat in Alberta is already planted., according to a telegraphic report of June 1. May I say to my hon. friends from Saskatchewan that the whole of their crop has been planted. I say, to the credit of the farmers of Saskatchewan, that notwithstanding climatic conditions, notwithstanding that, as I am given to understand, they had approximately three million acres of wheat that had not been threshed last year, they measured up to their responsibility and until the fall, I am informed, by the deputy minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan, they think the problem is well under the bridge. These are facts and not opinions. I am frank to admit that I do not understand as much about agriculture in its practical operation as some of the members who spoke this afternoon, but I do know, and I think the country should be told, what an admirable contribution

Man-Power-Mr. Mitchell

has been made by the farmers in every province of Canada to the war effort since the outbreak ' of hostilities.
I often used to say to my friends in the labour movement that if Hitler could be defeated by speeches and typewriters there would not have been any war, and I think it is a fair thing to say that you cannot plant wheat by making speeches. The farmers in the agricultural provinces have proved to the members of this House of Commons that while we have talked they have got on with the job, much to their undying credit.
I might refer now to the provinces that were discussed this afternoon-Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and largely Quebec.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: And Ontario.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Not much has been said about Ontario, but I shall come to that province. In the province of Quebec they, too, have been in difficulties owing to weather conditions. It has been cold and wet, and the report with reference to the province of Quebec is to the effect that those crops which are better because of wet conditions have improved. As a matter of fact, with their permit system in operation, all the persons who have been given temporary permits to go into industry during the winter season, when things are a little slack on the farms, have not yet been returned to agriculture, and the figures are rather illuminating. There were 2,127 temporary permits granted to go into other lines of work and vocations, and of that total, to date 620 have been cancelled; 1,057 have gone back to the farms voluntarily, and 879 permits have not been cancelled. So much for the province of Quebec.
Perhaps I should say a word with regard to cooperation between the provinces and the dominion. When people talk about manpower muddle as regards agriculture, it is fair to say that they do not know what they are talking about. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) put it clearly this afternoon when he said that it was much easier to state a problem than to solve it.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Would the minister give the Ontario figures, so as to complete the record?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I should be grateful if
my hon. friend would not interrupt my train of thought at the moment. I am speaking *extemporaneously.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
He does not interrupt
often.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I appreciate that. He
is in the next constituency to mine.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Is that a compliment to him?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It is a compliment to him. As I was saying, the hon. member for Weyburn remarked that it was much easier to state a problem than to solve it, and I think it is fair to say that in the evolutionary development of the man-power situation in this war the Canadian people will be found to have measured up with any other nation among the united nations. Make no mistake about that.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
In spite of the
government.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
My hon. friend, of
course, for political reasons would have to say, in spite of the government. I listened to him this afternoon and he was not quite as honest as I was, though I may have been out of the house part of the time he was speaking. However, like myself, I do not think he is an expert on agriculture. He said he admitted it, and I am glad he did. Let me say this. In cooperation with the provinces, the farmers' organizations and the federal government, I believe that everything that is humanly possible to enable us to deal adequately with the man-power problem, so far as the farms are concerned, has been done.
My hon. friend who comes from the province of Quebec moved this resolution, and I would point out to him that at this very moment there are 900 local committees working in complete harmony with the government of Quebec and the federal government to meet the problem. An hon. member speaks of Ontario. That province, let me say, through the farm organizations, and in every other way, has been working in complete harmony with us. Take the constituency represented by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). I have lived for many years close to it and I know it is a representative farming community of the best type in Ontario. The agricultural war committee is made up of representative farmers in the county, and they list no requirements for hired men by the year, estimating that 450 seasonal workers will be required. This estimate was made as late as May 4.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Who made that estimate.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
This is the committee
of local farmers. These are known as victory committees.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The minister had better
give me the names of those farmers later.

Man-Power-Mr. Mitchell

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I shall be glad to give the names of the committee. I could go through all the provinces in a similar manner. I have been careful to canvass the situation in the different provinces with ministers of agriculture, and I wish to be frank with the house, because, after all, wisdom is not all on this side, and I deeply appreciate some of the suggestions made by my hon. friends across the floor this afternoon.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Better be careful of these admissions.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Oh, I think we are all grown up men. We can understand that.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Will the minister put on the record the figures for other provinces, such as Manitoba?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I think I said that when we come to the main debate I will do that. I shall have more time. Of course I have to stay here as long as my hon. friends want me. As I said, I was speaking extemporaneously, and I did not mean to make a long statement this evening, but only to inform hon. members from various provinces who have spoken, of the condition of the crops in those various provinces, and what has been done.
This is from the minister of agriculture of British Columbia:
This department desires to express its appreciation of the early consummation of the dominion-provincial farm labour agreements which we feel sure -will prove helpful to agriculture generally. Result seeding should be made possible without great hardship. Compulsory transfer orders should when successfully carried out be of tremendous assistance and would respectfully suggest that mobilization regulations be definitely clarified in order to further agricultural production. Policy generally should be effective and believe that failing its adoption production could not have been maintained.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: What is the date of that telegram?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
This is a report to me on June 1. It may have come in a few days previously; I do not know.
Then, from Alberta, the provincial minister of agriculture reports that the dominion-provincial agreement will be helpful and that his department is prepared to give the fullest cooperation to make the joint programme a success. He does suggest that the effectiveness of the programme might have been considerably increased had the farm labour agreement been negotiated and approved at an earlier date. Reference is made in his reply to the additional task which farmers had this spring in completing threshing which had to be left over from last fall.
72537-211J
I think I quoted a telegraphic statement of the conditions of the crops in Alberta, which apparently is a little more hopeful than even this wire from the minister.
Then, from Saskatchewan:
Early completion dominion-provincial farm labour agreement has resulted in effective cooperation between dominion-provincial departments concerned. Seeding crop well advanced and will be completed with minimum delay but some individual hardship. Compulsory transfer orders have had limited value so far but should become more effective as season progresses.. Clarification of mobilization regulations has greatly assisted agriculture. Postponements to agricultural workers granted since February first major factor in seeding crops on farms affected. I believe present policy will result in labour being generally available for ordinary year around farm work but severe shortage at harvest time possible. Early plans for labour supply at that time imperative.
May I say to my hon. friends from Saskatchewan that I think their victory committees are doing a magnificent job there in the allocation of farm labour. I have always believed that the best form of government and the best organization is that which is closest to the people, and it is to the credit of our farmers' organizations that in every province of the dominion, when we ask for their cooperation we have got it. The seeding reports which I have received are a vindication of the work which in large measure has been undertaken by these victory committees in the province of Saskatchewan.
From Manitoba, the provincial minister of agriculture states that Manitoba farmers are unable to meet present competition for labour and pay current wages from farm revenues. He describes the farm help problem in Manitoba as an all-year round one, and suggests that more experienced help must be transferred back to agriculture from other industries. The minister makes the observation that the farm labour agreement is a step in the right direction and has resulted in the coordinaton of effort to secure farm help. He expresses appreciation for the cooperation received from the labour department.
As regards Ontario, the minister of agriculture for Ontario writes that the dominion-provincial agreements will be helpful in solving the farm labour problem, but points out that, according to estimates secured through the offices of the agricultural representatives, there is still a very great shortage of seasonal and year-round help. The minister states it is his conviction that there must be a return ' to the farms of much of the experienced help which has migrated into industry and the home defence units. He is not hopeful that the present move for the compulsory transfer
Man-Power-Mr. Mitchell

of men. back to agriculture will be of substantial benefit. He is of the opinion that some plan for subsidizing wages be offered to experienced farmers now in industry who might be brought back to agriculture.
The premier of Quebec stated in his wire that the "dominion-provincial agreement will be of great help to solve the Quebec farm labour problem." He mentions that late seeding has caused some difficulties, but these are being overcome. The premier believes that additional benefit might be secured through a further clarification of mobilization regulations so far as farm workers are concerned. He says that full use will be made of student labour which can be mobilized for farm work and advocates the temporary release of farmers' sons as well as experienced farm workers now taking military training.
As to New Brunswick, the dominion-provincial farm labour programme in New Brunswick is making good progress. A provincial director of the programme has been appointed and the agricultural field men for the province have been active with organization work. Close cooperation is being secured from the employment and selective service offices in New Brunswick.
As regards Nova Scotia, the provincial minister of agriculture regards the farm labour situation as critical. He advocates early release of farm labour now employed in other industry and asks that certain classes of men in the armed forces be released for temporary periods to assist with seeding and harvest. The use of Italian prisoners of war and conscientious objectors is recommended. The minister states that there has been an improvement in the administration of the mobilization regulations as they affect agricultural workers, but believes there is still room for further improvement. He offers the fullest cooperation of his department in the joint undertaking of the dominion and ,the province to meet the problem of farm labour.
The premier of Prince Edward Island suggests that the farm labour programme was organized too late for his province, but at the same time adds that the dominion-provincial agreement has been helpful in meeting the labour shortage on the farms. The premier states that as a result of the increased production of live stock and live-stock products the need for regular experienced help is a most diffcult one for farmers. He is sceptical about the effectiveness of the recent compulsory labour transfer orders in providing much assistance to agriculture. The reason cited for this conclusion is that little relief can be expected from directing inexperienced help to farms. The clarification of the mobilization regulations has been of assistance. The premier observes

that there is much dissatisfaction among farm labourers on account of the difference in wages paid in industry compared with those of agriculture.
A lot of ground has been covered in the debate this afternoon and evening. Much of it spills over into the Department of National Defence, and much of it, of course, is out of order in relation to the resolution which is before the house at the present time.
I can assure my hon. friends that when the whole man-power problem is discussed I shall look for their comments and, may I say, criticisms, for, after all is said and done, the essence of democracy is criticism. Without criticism democracy could not exist.
Further, may I point out that this nation is not the only one of the united nations- indeed, I may include the axis powers-which is at the moment facing a man-power problem. When that problem is discussed by the house I hope to be able to indicate the position in which Germany finds itself at the moment and to compare it with our own. Much the same conditions prevail in the United States and Great Britain. I am in fact convinced of this, that if we did not have a shortage of men for the army, the navy, the air force, agriculture, industry, the mines, the base metals, and lumbering, this country would not be doing its duty in the present grave emergency. The fact that we have a shortage is a reflection of the contribution of this dominion on behalf of the united nations in the present struggle.
In the years to come I for one will look back with pride on the contribution made by the people of this dominion. We have had almost a revolution in the application of our man-power policies as they affect the Canadian people. Whoever thought we would live to see the day when well nigh all the manpower and woman-power of this country would pass through the employment service; that we would reach the point where in the great majority of cases we deny the individual the right to advertise in the newspapers for a job? That in itself is a revolution among a democratic people. Whoever thought we would live to see the day when a man would have to give seven days' notice before he could quit a job and when an employer would have to give seven days' notice before he could discharge a man? I know that in Germany and other countries where dictatorships exist, these things are taken as matters of course, but these are new policies to the freedom-loving people of this dominion, who I think are without a peer in the world when it comes to an appreciation of the basic principles of

Man-Power-Mr. Mitchell
freedom. Whoever thought that in the short space of six months these people would willingly-and I speak now in a broad way, of course-accept these changes? Of course there will be exceptions to that rule; we will get letters from people who think we have gone too far, but let us not forget that simply reading a letter in this House of Commons does not make it true. It is the easiest thing in the world to take the word of someone else before due investigation is made.
Some hon. gentlemen have expressed criticism-perhaps rightly so; I do not know-in regard to the application of the call-up for. compulsory military training. I think when the figures are brought to their attention, at leaist since the latest policies have gone into operation, there will be very little criticism offered. But let me point out one fact. I would not want it to be said about any administration over which I presided that any vocation, any form of employment, could be made a hideaway, as it were, for people1 who should be meeting their obligations to the country. So that I say to hon. members: When you get these letters, at least give us a chance, because I think, speaking in a broad way, the work of these mobilization boards has constantly improved. As one hon. member from near Quebec city said this afternoon, they are an improvement over the boards which functioned during the last war. I do not say that with any desire to criticize the boards that functioned at that time, because in connection with many of our policies we have built on the mistakes of the past. That is the logical thing to do. I think our conception of the length of this war has been beclouded by the length of the last war. I am one of those who still think this war is going to last a long time. I am one of those who still think much more direction will have to be given our people before the man-power problem of this country is finally dealt with in an efficient way. Last fall it was my good fortune to be in Britain. Mr. Bevin, the minister of labour there, has, I suppose, even more power on paper than I have on paper, but notwithstanding that power ninety-five per cent of the movement of men and women in industry has been on a voluntary basis and compulsion has been necessary only in regard to the remaining five per cent.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Could the minister tell us how that result was achieved? Was it not through close cooperation with the labour organizations?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Since I have had charge of the direction of selective service, every move I have made has been in consultation with representatives of the employers and the
workers of this country, through the national selective service advisory board. I do not think it serves any good purpose to say that we do not consult anyone. I speak for my own department, of course, but in every step I have made I have endeavoured to consult with the representatives of both employers and employees. I think there are well over three hundred representatives of these two very necessary parts of our industrial and agricultural structure serving on various boards under my jurisdiction, and I have always found it far more satisfactory to get their sage advice before moving in the direction in which we would like to move.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Has any use been made of the trade unions by selective service, where transfers have to be made?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I think we are very close to the trade unions; probably my hon. friend knows that.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: That is what we do not know.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have just stated that any move is taken after consultation. I should say, however, that sometimes you must move with expedition, in an emergency; sometimes you cannot wait. If my hon. friend were sitting here instead of there, perhaps he would be a little more rigorous than I have been. However, we have endeavoured to obtain the friendly advice of the trade unions in the operation of selective service. Sometimes it is rather difficult to give advice when occasionally you must be a couple of steps ahead of your own people, but to the credit of both great partners in industry I think it can be said that they have measured up to their responsibilities in connection with the selective service programme of the federal government, and I do not think it would be fair if I did not pay them this tribute.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have pretty well covered all I wish to say at the moment, though I could say more. Something has been said about the loss of production. I could mention what is occurring in the various provinces, and perhaps it would be as well if I did.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Having given the
figures in connection with one province, the minister must have the figures for the other provinces. Could we not have them also? It would take only a moment to put them on record.
Man-Power-Mr. Mitchell

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will sympathize with me, because in the first place I was given no notice that this debate was coming on this afternoon.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: But the minister has the figures for one province.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Yes; I collected a few things, but later I shall have a complete manpower statement to make. I think it was the leader of the opposition who asked that this statement be forthcoming.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I certainly did.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: It will be given when I have an opportunity to db so. I am in the hands of the house; I have not been able to get on as soon as I should have liked, but my hon. friend may rest assured that I shall give any figures I can get.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The minister has the figures for one province.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I have no other figures before me. I am trying to get these figures up to the latest possible date, because the later they are the better. This statement in regard to provinces shows that in Prince Edward Island the percentage of cows milking to total numbers showed a marked increase in the month of March. The number of calves born was somewhat higher'than that of the same month last year. In Nova Scotia more cows were reported on farms in the month of March. In New Brunswick the production of milk exceeded that of March. In Quebec there was no apparent change in the number of cows available for milking purposes. In Ontario a subsidy was offered for butter, and there has been increased milk production. Many farmers have been forced to change their plans on account of the labour shortage. In Manitoba the total production of milk increased. In Saskatchewan more milk was produced in March than in the same month of 1942. In Alberta cow numbers showed a substantial advance in March over those of the same month last year, and more cows were freshened for milking purposes.
And so, Mr. Speaker, I believe I have more or less effectively-at least I hope I have-1 answered the questions asked by my horn, friends this afternoon. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) said the forms necessary to fill out in connection with the compulsory call-up for military service are difficult to understand. I believe when I give the latest figures respecting the number of postponements, particularly in connection with agriculture, he will not find them so .difficult.

I think I need not say more at the present time, except this:	This has been a debate
respecting agriculture, and on- behalf of the House of Commons I should like to pay tribute to the cooperation, the hard work and, in many instances, the sacrifice of the farmers in this great dominion.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say a word
at this stage in the debate respecting our position in connection with this motion for the adjournment of the house. We have been attempting to follow, as best we can, the procedure laid down>-true, in an informal way, but nevertheless laid down'-under which we would deal, department after department, with the war appropriation bill. There may have been times when there have been deviations from that informal arrangement. Nevertheless it has seemed to me that the most important measure before the house at this session has been, without any shadow of a doubt, the war appropriation bill. This party has felt that the man-power problem, in its relation to the war appropriation measure, was perhaps the major one to be faced at this time. It was that thought which prompted my suggesting to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) last week that, after the estimates of the three armed services had been discussed1 we should put aside our other business and proceed at once with the estimates of the Department of Labour, thereby affording ourselves an opportunity to come to grips with the man-power problem in Canada, a problem which we may justifiably regard as the chief one facing us to-day.
I was rather surprised this afternoon when I learned of the motion which, first of all, would deal with the man-power problem in a piecemeal fashion and, second, would have the inevitable result of delaying for another day the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). For these reasons I point out to the house that in my opinion we would have been better as a House of Commons, urgent as this matter is, to have at least dealt with it on a broad front, and a front which would have brought some results at the conclusion of debate. I believe the problem of man-power cannot be divided into departments. What has been done this afternoon has been to take one department, regardless of the whole.
While sitting in my seat this afternoon, listening to debate, I could not help wondering how much farm help we were giving our farmers in Canada through the talk to which

Man-Power-Mr. Gray don
*we have listened during the afternoon and evening. To my mind there is only one way in which we can help the farmers with their labour problems, and that is to give them help.
I do not agree with the minister, nor do I agree with some other hon. members who spoke this afternoon who seem to hold the view that the farmer does not need help. Those of us coming from agricultural constituencies know that he does.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend heard me say that the farmer does not need help.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The minister said a number of things to-night when he was speaking; but may I say to the minister that he left the definite impression that things were not so very bad, so far as agriculture is concerned. If he will say to-night that things are good, in connection with the agricultural help situation, then I would like him to say it.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I thought I made it plain to my hon. friend. I had not thought I created the impression he has indicated. If I did, then I certainly did not intend to. A man would be foolish to do that, under present circumstances. But I do say what I have said before, offering it as a tribute with all the sincerity in my being, and in the knowledge that we are all cooperating together, that notwithstanding the serious problem we are up against we are producing more than ever was produced in the history of this country. Surely that is to the credit of the farmers. I am frank to admit that in the very nature of things, when you have close to a couple of million people in the armed forces and in industry, you cannot have as many people on the farms. That is an actual fact-and the same condition exists in every other country in the world.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I am glad to have the minister correct what I thought was the impression he had created in connection with the agricultural man-power policy. But he read very carefully telegrams and reports from various governmental departments in the provinces. Certainly, so far as my knowledge goes, the problem indicated in those reports in connection with man-power seemed to be a very simple one compared with the problem which is presented to members of parliament from time to time.
I say to the minister that he will find prevalent in the agricultural sections of the dominion a condition such as has never existed at any previous time in our history. He will find that there never before has been
a time when farmers, their wives and families were so completely played out with hard work as they are to-day. I make that statement from personal experience because, as the minister knows, I have gone among them. I do not think I have ever seen the farming people more tired than they are to-day, and that condition has arisen largely because they have not been able to get the help necessary to operate their farms.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member, and I think it would be safe to say the same about the men and women engaged in industry.	_

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: We are not dealing with industry just now, but I would be glad to agree with his statement about the people engaged in industry. But when we talk about emergent conditions, and when we are confronted with a motion for adjournment to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, then I say that the problem of farm help was urgent months ago. It was urgent weeks ago; it was urgent yesterday; it is urgent to-day, and unless government policy is changed, it will be urgent to-morrow and in the months ahead. I should like to point out to those who are responsible for bringing up this motion that, so far as urgency is concerned, this motion is both too little and too late.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Why did you not start something before?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: My hon. friend made a very good speech and I am doing my best to keep up with him. There is no doubt that this question is urgent, but I repeat that it has been urgent for some time. In my opinion the policy of the government with respect to national selective service must be changed. This is not the time in the interests of the farmer to bring up this matter. I say that plainly and clearly. If I thought that we as a party could do something this afternoon or this evening for the farmer by simply talking about this matter, then we might take a different stand. But we are not doing anything by simply moving the adjournment of the house. During the debate on the estimates of the minister we shall have a chance at least to fight this thing through. I wish to say to the minister that, so far as our group is concerned, we have made some preparation to fight this thing through.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: Where will you get?

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
You have not got very far, but we still have hopes. I say to the ministry that we wish to come to grips with the whole question of the man-power policy.
Man-Power-Mr. Graydon

We want to do that at as early a date as possible, and that is why we have not tried this afternoon to delay the house. I hope the house will understand our reasons for taking this action.
There is no question that the policy of the government with respect to man-power has been muddled, misconceived and misfitted; but I should like to reserve my remarks with respect to that for a more suitable time when the whole problem, integrated1 as it is with industry and the armed forces, can be properly discussed. I hope that we will have considerable support from the house in that connection.
This motion provides only a palliative for agriculture, and I do not think we want to spend much time on palliatives. I should have liked to see the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) put some teeth into this, as we hope to put teeth into it when we deal with man-power. I should have liked to see him rise in his place and do something more than move a milk-and-water resolution such as this. I should have liked to see the hon. member come through with a proper national selective service scheme, one which would have brought labour to the farms of Canada and not bring up something which has resulted simply in a lengthy debate which can give no help whatever to the farmers generally.
Mr. POULIOT; At the beginning of the session I sent to each hon. member an article which I had written on national selective service, and if the hon. member did not have his copy translated, it is his own fault.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I think I have received everything the hon. member has sent me, and I thank him for his courtesy. I have given it close study and attention, and part of my remarks to-night are based on the study I have given to matters of this kind in general.
In closing, I wish to say to the government to beware of the existing situation. There are reasons behind the movement which has taken place this afternoon. One of them is that the government have failed to deal manfully with the man-power problem. We as a party take a back seat to no one, whether he has moved this or supported it, in our desire to see the farmers of Canada provided with adequate labour in the months that lie ahead. That is part of our policy. We may differ in the method of bringing it about. We hope to take some action that will bring results and give help to the farmers which I am doubtful will be given by talking in the House of Commons for a whole day and delaying a debate which we are waiting for and which we hope to be ready for when the time comes.

maintopic: MAN-POWER MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I shall, at the outset, congratulate the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) on the timely action he has taken this afternoon, in moving the adjournment of the house for the discussion of the serious problem which agriculture is facing on account of the present labour shortage. This is not the first occasion on which the hon. member for Temiscouata has rendered a service to his country. During this session he has made numerous remarks and speeches which have been quite effective but which could have been still more helpful, had the oligarchy which rules the country at this time been more willing to accept the good suggestions he offered. As I said, I congratulate him on his action and I hope it will bring about very good results.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has just deprecated the action of the hon. member for Temiscouata. His criticism surprises me very much. If agriculture is in such a serious plight as has been stated, and it must be true, if the hon. members of this house, whatever their political affiliations may be, whether they be Liberal Conservative, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, or Social Credit, who took part in the debate and represent various rural constituencies all over the -country are aware of local conditions. I believe it was quite helpful that such representations should have been -made to the government, in view of the fact that the seeding season is now so far advanced, as was stated this afternoon by the hon. member for Labelle, who I notice is now smiling. If the government would heed the representations that have been made by the hon. members and disregard the concerted oligarchy this government represents, and which will take -advice from no one, the nation would perhaps not be so often confronted with problems as alarming as the one which it is now facing, the famine problem. In the light of what I have read in the newspapers and heard from hon. members of this house, I feel that if common sense prevailed, as well as a determination to- do the right thing, with a view -to serving the country efficiently and helping our allies in the war, if such a spirit moved all cabinet members the useful suggestions that were made would immediately have produced good results, and the leader of the opposition would not have referred to the futility or the uselessness of the present debate.
There is a labour shortage in Canadian agriculture. That is unquestionable. The numerous letters we receive from farmers

Man-Power-Mr. Roy
who ask us to endeavour to secure the release of their sons from military service are proof of this. There are a great many others. I have here a copy of the June 1, 1943, edition of the Montreal newspaper La Presse in which is reported a speech delivered in New York on that date by the hon. the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand) of whom I caught a glimpse as he entered the- house and to whom I am glad to extend my greetings. He discussed the problem brought about by the labour shortage, while dealing with fisheries. I wish to quote the following passage from the newspaper report I mentioned a few moments ago:
New York, June 1 (C.P.)-Owing to the labour shortage fish production in Canada this year may be reduced to 750,000,000 pounds as compared with 923,000,000 pounds in 1941, it was stated here to-day by the Hon. Ernest Bertrand, Minister of Fisheries in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I believe I am in order in dealing with fisheries and fish, because the motive which prompted the motion introduced this afternoon, namely the labour shortage in agriculture, is indeed based on the shortage of foodstuffs in this country. Fisheries automatically come up alongside agriculture in this debate because foodstuffs are also derived from them. Further on, the honourable the Minister of Fisheries referred to the lack of young men and the labour shortage in the fishing industry. He said1:
On the other hand, the problem is serious, because we have lost a considerable number of our young and most efficient fishermen who have enlisted in the army and the navy. Many others are employed in war plants, and quite a number of small fishing boats have been chartered for war patrol duties. On one side, there is an enormous demand, and on the other, a shortage of labour and equipment.
According to a statement of the hon. Minister of Fisheries, there is likely to be a decrease in the fish production this year, due to a scarcity of man-power attributable, so he states, to the fact that men have gone to the war industries or have been conscripted into the army.
The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) proved this fact a while ago, but I doubt that this was the best argument in favour of the point he was attemping to make. Answering criticisms of the government policy, especially National War Services, of which I shall have a word to say later, the hon. Minister of Labour stated that the call-up of men for the army was not the only reason for the present scarcity of man-power. A large number of farmers, farmers' sons and farm employees, during the relatively slack winter season, asked permission to work in the war
industries and have neglected to return to the farm. While I am on this question of work in the war industries, I shall point out that these men have not yet been released from their jobs, which they still hold, as suggested by the statement of the hon. minister. If they have not yet been sent on the farm or elsewhere, it is of course because industry needs them. Canada is expected to be alone responsible for winning the war. A sufficient number of men had to be trained and a fairly large number had to be sent overseas so as to be in a position to win the war by themselves. Moreover, Canada was to be the arsenal and the granary of all countries and supply allied nations with all they require in the way of munitions and armaments in order to win the war. At the same time, Canada was to feed the entire population of Great Britain because they are waging war and have suffered from air raids. It has also just been realized-and I wish to stress the point-that Canada should also feed the starving people of India and of China. The hon. minister replied to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) that rationing was established not because of a shortage of potatoes but because we must think of China and remember that others go without. I would point out to the hon. Minister of Labour that although China had known poverty, hardship and famine prior to 1941, until then neither the minister nor the present government had ever thought of sending our food surpluses to China.
Never has the hon. minister or the present cabinet thought of sending there the food surpluses that were glutting our markets even in the west, and this applies to our butter which was so abundant, that its marketing offered quite a serious challenge to the administration a few years ago. No one has ever thought of sending our food surpluses to China, a country which was as much in need then as it is tq-day. It is only after Canada, England and the United States declared war on Japan that this thought came to our minds. That is why such arguments make little impression and do not always carry conviction.
I revert to the colossal undertaking which consists in playing the game of our ambitious industrialists, by increasing production as well as profits, as we know, and by organizing a huge aripy, of a size comparable to that of vastly more populous countries; the hon. minister himself foresaw, as he stated in the course of last year's debate on bill 80, the conscription bill so-called, that deficiencies would develop in certain fields, unless we were very careful.
Still another minister was of the same opinion. I mean the then Minister of National
Doctor Eduard Benes

War Services, Mr. Thorson, who is now replaced by the hon. Minister of Labour to a certain extent. He stated, as reported in Hansard for 1942:
Furthermore, our war industry programme contemplates and involves heavy man-power requirements. So does the programme for essential agricultural production. I shall not deal in detail with either of these programmes, except to say that the man-power necessary for their performance cannot be withdrawn from the essential purposes of war without hurting those purposes.
It is the duty of the government to allocate man-power in accordance with the needs of the war purposes of Canada and the war objectives that I have mentioned.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

maintopic: DOCTOR EDUARD BENES

speechtext: Address of His Excellency Doctor Eduard Benes, President of Czechoslovakia, to members of the Senate and of the House of Commons, in the Railway Committee room, House of Commons, Ottawa, Thursday, June 3, 1943, at 12 noon.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DOCTOR EDUARD BENES
speechtext:
We in Canada are indeed greatly honoured to have in our country today His Excellency Doctor Eduard Benes, the President of the Republic of Czechoslovakia. I wish at once to extend to Doctor Benes the warmest of welcomes on behalf of the government, the parliament and the people of Canada. Doctor Benes is such a well-known international figure and has played such a prominent part in world events over the past three decades that he does not come to us in any sense a stranger, and needs no introduction to any democratic audience in any part of the world.
I should like to say to Doctor Benes what I said in the House of Commons yesterday, that he will have noticed a very close sympathy between the people of Canada and the people of the Czechoslovak republic. The agreement at Munich, which had the effect of partitioning his country and caused great sacrifices on the part of his people, sacrifices made, it was thought at the time, in the interests of the whole of Europe but which have since proved to have been on behalf of the whole world- that agreement was never recognized by Canada and is not recognized by Canada today.
We share in regard to Czechoslovakia the view of the British government that the Munich agreement has ceased to exist as a factor either in present or post-war relations.

We look forward to the day, which we hope is coming speedily, when the Czechoslovak republic in its entirety will again be restored to its full independence.
One expression, Mr. President, which we have sought to give to our feelings of close relationship with the people and government of Czechoslovakia has been to welcome to Canada Doctor Erantisek Pavlasek, who is seated to my left, as minister of /the Republic of Czechoslovakia, and to appoint in London a minister from Canada to the country of which you are presently the head. I would take advantage of this opportunity to say how greatly Doctor Pavlasek as minister of Czechoslovakia has endeared himself to all those who have had the privilege of making his acquaintance while here. As you yourself told me, Mr. President, when we recently talked together in Washington, Doctor Pavlasek was a close friend of the founder of your great republic, Masaryk, the country of which you are a co-founder and that he was one of the most cultured gentlemen in Czechoslovakia. We here have come to appreciate through the personality of Doctor Pavlasek and in his public utterances not only much of the culture of Czechoslovakia but also the high ideals of your country.
I am not going to take time this morning to say more than one other word by way of welcome to Doctor Benes. It is that we welcome him not only as representing the brave people of Czechoslovakia and the great services they have rendered to democracy but we welcome him also and in great measure at this moment on account of himself. He has a career of public service that has been paralleled' by very few men in the world's history. As all present know he was co-founder of the Republic of Czechoslovakia. He was the first Foreign Minister of that country and has been its President for many years. He bore the heaviest responsibilities throughout the trying period of the Munich discussions and the years which followed, a time when his country was passing through a terrible ordeal. He did all within his power to keep united the forces of freedom in his own and other lands. It is of interest to know that he came at that very time to America and was for a very short period associated with the university of Chicago. He found there a sphere from which as President in exile from his country he might be able to direct its affairs in its titanic struggle for freedom. He has, as you know, been responsible for the organization of the different forces of Czechoslovakia. I should like to say to him how much the people of Canada in common with people everywhere who love liberty appreciate the

Doctor Eduard Benes
great services which Czechoslovakia rendered to the cause of freedom in the last great war and the great services she has never ceased to render to the cause of freedom since and in the present war.
Czechoslovakia has had to bear some of the heaviest burdens any country has ever been called upon to endure by way of sacrifice for a great cause. These she bore at the time of Munich. These she ha3 borne ever since. These she is bearing heroically to-day. Notwithstanding that at present the country is occupied by the enemy, her forces both within Czechoslovakia and in different parts of the world, are fighting in the cause of freedom with the allied and united nations of the world. That is a great tradition for a nation and we know that that heroic effort is going to win its due reward.
I need not touch on other aspects of Doctor Benes' career, of his presidency of the Assembly of League of Nations and of course his leadership at the present time of his government in exile. From the beginning and all through his life he has been the exponent of high and noble ideals and of those great aims, purposes and practical measures which seek not only the higher development of the peoples of his own country but also fraternity and unity between all nations.
When I was recently at Washington I asked Doctor Benes how it was that he came to venture on some of the prophecies that he had made, prophecies which are giving much in the way of hope to the world at this time. He said to me, in reply, that the so-called prophecies were not in reality prophecies, that as a matter of fact he has had the good fortune, in the many years he has been in public life, to form intimate friendships with men in many countries and had been particularly fortunate in being able for the most part to keep up these friendships through the period of the war, and that from information he had gathered at first hand in this way he has ventured to give open expression to some of the views which he holds regarding the present and the future.
I should like in this connection to read a statement that Doctor Benes publicly made before the war actually took place. All of us would, I think, regard it as a prophecy. Doctor Benes himself would say that it is based on logic and philosophy and expresses only a sequence of facts gathered from the confidences of the acquaintances he has maintained.
In November, 1938, the gentleman who this morning is seated to my right made the following statement in regard to what he believed was likely to happen within a short
time after the Munich agreement had been entered into. He said at that time that he believed war was inevitable after Munich. He went on:
I do not know when it will break out, possibly in a year, perhaps in two or three. I personally doubt whether it will take more than a year.
This was in November, 1938. The attack on Poland came on September 1, 1939.
The first to suffer the blow will be Poland.
. . . France will pay horribly. . . . Hitler will attack all-in the west, and even Russia-and in the end America, too, will be in it.
I do not think I need say anything further by way of introduction of the President of the Czechoslovak republic as one who is entitled to speak with great authority on international affairs.

maintopic: DOCTOR EDUARD BENES
speechtext:
Mr. Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Mr. Speaker of the House of Commons: Let me first thank you very warmly and sincerely for the kind words with which I have been introduced to this distinguished audience.
It is the first time in the history of Canadian-Czechoslovak relations that a president of Czechoslovakia has the honour of addressing the Canadian parliament. I am cognizant of the great historical significance of this event, and I am profoundly grateful that the honour is mine.
The great contribution of Canada to the struggle of the world for the defeat of German nazism and for the reestablishment of liberty, the achievements this country has made in her war, the organization of her army, navy and air force, industrial and especially financial success in solving extremely difficult war problems, the steadiness and the spirit of this country, evoke a deep and sincere admiration.
The sympathy of the Canadian government and people for Czechoslovakia, expressed in words and deeds during the past four years, has been an encouragement and inspiration in this darkest period of modern Czechoslovak history.
You know that for centuries beginning with the middle ages this small nation in the heart of Europe had been a glorious independent kingdom and a prosperous state. The state that first began the fight for religious freedom in Europe. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Prague, its capital, was a great centre of learning, contributed largely to European cultural, spiritual and material development, and played an outstanding role in European history and particularly in the history of the Holy Roman Empire and the
Doctor Eduard Benes

Austro-Hungarian monarchy. Perhaps your government knew, too, the famous declaration made by the German Chancellor Bismarck after his victory over Austria in 1866: Whoever is master of Bohemia, is master of Europe. Europe must, therefore, never allow any nation except the Czechs to rule it, since that nation does not lust for domination. The boundaries of Bohemia are the safeguard of European security and he who moves them will plunge Europe into misery.
In my estimation there can be no better comment on the position of my country even to-day.
The recognition of our cause here in this country in 191S was also undoubtedly due to the unmistakable determination of our people to live as a free and independent nation. More than one hundred and fifty thousand Czechoslovak soldiers, many of whom came from Canada to Europe, fought for their country's liberation in the first world war in Russia, France and Italy. When the war was drawing to a close, the epic march of the Czechoslovak legionnaires across the Siberian plains to Vladivostok fired the imagination of the Canadian people as well as the rest of the world. The first unit of our legionnaires made its way across the Pacific from Russia to the battlefields of France, landed in Vancouver and was enthusiastically welcomed by the Canadian people.
Czechoslovakia's twenty years' record as a free and independent democratic state is one of which we are justly proud. Surrounded on all sides by authoritarian countries and governments, she remained faithful to the democratic traditions which came to her very largely from the western hemisphere. Her social legislation and her educational system were progressive and advanced; her financial system was stable, her currency, one of the soundest in Europe; her general economic standard was very high and her import and export trade greater than that of Italy. Until 1938 this republic was one of the most prosperous and happy countries in Europe. Even the concentrated campaign of nazi Germany, beginning in 1936, using corruption, lying propaganda and threatening war and violence, failed to shake the inner harmony of the Czechoslovak republic.
In her foreign policy Czechoslovakia resolutely and consistently followed the policy of peace, international arbitration and collective security. She fostered and encouraged friendship with her neighbours-* Austria, Poland, Yugoslavia, and Rumania. She was the most loyal member of the League of Nations. She supported the Locarno policy, was an original signatory of [Dr. Eduard Benes.]
the Briand-Kellogg pact, and was ready to play the part demanded of her in any generally accepted system of collective security. In Geneva she resolutely opposed the Japanese invasion of Manchuria and China; I was President of the Assembly of the League of Nations when we voted the sanctions against Italy upon her invasion of Abyssinia. Czechoslovakia was ready to oppose militarily the occupation of the Rhineland and Austria. Our army and air force were ready and thoroughly efficient. Up to the year 1939 we did our duty completely, not only to our nation, but to Europe and democracy as well.
Czechoslovakia was in mortal danger from the moment that Hitler and the nazi leaders came to power. When Hitler saw that the policy of sanctioning against Italy was not strictly applied and when the German remilitarization of the Rhineland was not opposed by force, he thought that the countless seeds of bitterness and mistrust sown by the dictators would permit him to reap a harvest of	destruction	of democracy	inEurope and bring about the realization of his pan-German	plan. The	success	of the	annexation of	Austria in	March	led to	the
September crisis in 1938.
My own view then was that Hitler's demands and attacks against Czechoslovakia should have been rejected even at the cost of a war. We had ready one and a half million splendid soldiers. But the western powers were not ready for war in 1938,	either	morally,	or
materially. Through the sacrifice made by Czechoslovakia, Europe and the world gained a year's time in which to prepare better for the defence against the coming onslaught. In my opinion, the second world war began with the criminal occupation of Prague. And from the very day of occupation, March 15, 1939, all Czechoslovak citizens have been at war with Germany.
Since 1938 the Czechoslovaks at home have endured great hardships, sorrows and suffering. They know that many of their soldiers and airmen who escaped from their enslaved homeland lost their lives while fighting for its liberation in Poland and in France. They know that after the Franco-German armistice, Czechoslovak soldiers and airmen reassembled in Great Britain, and that in the decisive battle of Britain, Czechoslovak airmen played an honourable part. They know that Czechoslovak soldiers are now fighting in Russia and in Africa and manning the defences of Great Britain even while they see their own country being converted into an arsenal for a war against the united nations. Many are now

Doctor Eduard Benes
working as forced labourers in Germany and elsewhere. Those who resist the oppressors are either executed in masses or tortured in prisons and concentration camps. Their country is pillaged and germanized, their national education completely destroyed. The undying memory of the martyred village of Lidice forbids us ever to relax in the world-struggle now waged against the powers of evil and darkness.
We know what we are fighting for. Our every effort is. first of all, spent for the restoration of our democratic way of life, for those moral values that are fundamental to it, as opposed to the nazi creed which deprives individuals and nations not only of freedom but of human dignity and equality. We are fighting, too, for the return of international order, in which the sanctity of treaties and the pledged word will prevail, in contrast to their deliberate violation whenever the nazis consider it expedient. We are fighting for some sort of international charter-a charter which shall embody the rights of man and be applicable to the people of all countries; in short, for a world that is new and free. In my opinion, this entails the punishment of all those people who are guilty of perpetrating numberless crimes and cruelties of the past four years-not in the spirit of vengeance, but with a full measure of justice.
Secondly, we are fighting for a social and economic reorganization of the European continent, which will be in great danger of chaos and disruption after the present war. The ionsequences of this war will be far-reaching and social and economic difficulties far greater than those of 1918 in Europe. The democratic united nations will have the duty to remain politically and militarily together even after the present war. But the peace which comes after this war will necessitate their new close collaboration also in the social and economic spheres.
Thirdly, we are fighting for a more lasting peace in the future, one which will be guaranteed effectively by an international organization. A new system of collective security must be prepared and established, one which will be more practical and function more effectively than the last. The first steps have already been made in the treaty signed by the united nations, but more discussion and preparations on the far-reaching questions of peace will be necessary before unity among the united nations will be achieved.
This is directly connected with the fourth fundamental aim of the present war, the one which will perhaps be the most difficult and
at the same time most decisive to realize: a new political reorganization of Europe and the world. All these aims are interrelated and inseparable.
All the united nations, the great British commonwealth in which Canada has so vital a part and which has played such a glorious role in the present war; your great neighbour, the United States, whose friendly three-thousand mile boundary is an example of good neighbourliness to the rest of the world; Soviet Russia, who first broke the legend of nazi invincibility; China, whose strength seems incredibly increased as we look back on her heroic fight against the Japanese aggressors, as well as the smaller united nations, all share in this global struggle and all agree in these four great peace aims, which must be achieved in this second world war. Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Greece, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg, Norway, Austria as well as France-all have to be liberated. France has had to come to humiliating terms with the enemy. Even to-day the enemy has not exacted his last full measure of humiliation and vengeance. Germany has torn up the armistice agreement, imprisoned her manhood, or compelled it to work at forced labour. Yet France has never ceased to be capable of greatness. I believe that before very long France will rejoin her allies as a fully sovereign and belligerent nation. She will take her place at a council table of Europe. Europe needs a strong and regenerated France-and the same is true of the other subjugated nations-and without her there will be no lasting peace on the European continent.
After the collapse of Germany the united nations must, in my opinion, remain an organized body which will create the basis for the new post-war international order and for the new system of international collaboration and security, in which every member will play its due and proportionate part.
All Czechoslovaks are greatly indebted to Canada as well as to Great Britain and to the British commonwealth for the magnanimity with which she received Czechoslovak citizens who fled from their homeland in the past several years. They only followed their fellow countrymen who came years before to establish themselves permanently in Canada and are now faithful Canadian citizens and true Canadian patriots. I firmly believe that they are fully sharing Canada's effort in this war and will always serve to promote and strengthen our mutual understanding and friendship.
Doctor Eduard Benes

Canadians of Czechoslovak origin are now fighting in the Canadian and partly in the Czechoslovak army abroad. Many fliers, Canadian and Czechoslovak, trained here in your great country, are bravely fighting together to defeat our common enemy, who brought this war upon us.
Czechoslovakia's gratitude for Canada's consistent policy toward Czechoslovakia since 1918 is boundless. Mr. Mackenzie King's repudiation of the wanton German aggression against Czechoslovakia in the House of Commons on March 20, 1939, Canada's refusal to recognize the occupation of Czechoslovakia on April 7, 1941, and the granting of full recognition to the government of Czechoslovakia in England on July 17, 1942, has been the rounding out of this mutual relationship. These are ties that bind Canada and Czechoslovakia together and will bind them forever; and my thanks for all this, Mr. Prime Minister, to you, to your Parliament, and to your great country.
Czechoslovakia's policy has not changed since 1918. Nor will it change after victory is ours. I feel authorized to declare on behalf of my nation that after the final victory in this great war is achieved, the Czechoslovak nation will reconstruct its old home rapidly and successfully by its untiring efforts, remaining faithful-as it always was during the difficult periods of its long, chequered and glorious history-to the democratic way of life, to the principles of spiritual and religious freedom and to the ideals of peace and peaceful international collaboration, of which Canada and its brave and1 freedom-loving people was always one of the most typical and courageous representatives in the policy of the whole world.
